speechtext:
This Bill stood for the purpose of further consideration of provisions made with regard to certain changes in the description of constituencies in the province of Quebec. It was then suggested that instead of the form in which the Bill then was, in so far as it modified the description of the constituencies of Quebec East and Quebec West and Jacques Cartier, we 'should adopt as more desirable the form of repealing the sections and substituting other sections containing the proposed alterations.
I have had this done, and 1 now beg to move that section 4 as it was in the Bill that was presented to the House be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
4.	Number 6 (b), the description of the electoral district of Quebec East, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
" (b) The electoral district of Quebec East which shall consist of the following wards of the city of Quebec to wit: St. John, Jacques Cartier, St. Roch and Limoilou, exclusive of the village of Stadacona."
The change made there is simply the exclusion of the village of Stadacona. Quebec West will now read as follows:
5.	Number 6 (e), the description of the electoral district of Quebec West, is repealed and the fallowing is substituted therefor:
"(c) The electoral district of Quebec West which shall consist of the following wards of the city of Quebec to wit: St. Sauveur, St. Valier and St. Malo and the village of Stadacona and the municipality of Petite Riviere.
The amendment that is made there consists in the insertion of the village of Stadacona, and the words " the municipality of Petite Riviere." In the Bill sought to be amended it would have appeared that Petite RivRre was a ward instead of a municipality.
I beg also to move an amendment to section 5. The amendment to the existing Act sought to be made is the exclusion from the electoral district of Jacques Cartier of St. Denis ward, which, under the Act passed last year, forms a part of another constituency. The section that dealt with Jacques Cartier in the Bill as introduced was section 5, but it now becomes section 6, because we have taken in two sections to deal with the electoral district of Quebec East and Quebec West. Section 5 has now been struck out, and the following substituted as section 6:
Number 10 (a), the description of the electoral district of Jacques Cartier, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
" (a) The electoral district of Jacques Cartier which shall be constituted as at present less the town of Verdun, Outremont, any part of St. Denis ward-
It is intended to exclude the whole of St. Denis ward.

YTes. What was wrong with the Act was that St. Denis ward was not excluded as it should have been. I beg to move that section 6 of the Bill as introduced be struck out, and that the following be substituted as section 7:
Number 14 (a), the description of the electoral district of Hull, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
"(a) The electoral district of Hull shall consist of Hull city, East and West Hull, the municipality of South Hull, Gatineau Point, East and West Templeton, the town of Buckingham, the township of Buckingham, the township of Southeast Buckingham, the township of North Templeton, L'Ange Gardien, Portland East and West, Derry, Bowman, Villeneuve East and West, Blake, McGill, B gelow, Wells, Wabassee and Dudley.
The effect of this is to add to the description of Hull, as it stands in the existing law, the townships of South East Buckingham, North Templeton and the municipality of South Hull. As the present Bill was introduced it only provided for the inclusion in Hull of Southeast Buckingham and North Templeton, in addition to those mentioned in the Act as it stood. I understand that it was considered that it properly should include the municipality of South Hull, and I am now moving to include in the description of the electoral district the municipalities of Southeast Buckingham, North Templeton and South Hull. That necesitates amendments in regard to the electoral districts of Labelle and Wright, because these portions which are included in Hull are, under the existing Act, included in Labelle and Wright. Southeast Buckingham is included in Labelle, and North Templeton and South Hull are included in Wright. Therefore, to make the descriptions of Labelle and Wright consistent with these changes, I beg to move that section 8 be as follows:
Number 14 (b), the description of the electoral district of Labelle, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
" (b) The electoral district of Labelle which shall be constituted as at present less the town of Buckingham, the township of Buckingham, the township of Southeast Buckingham, L'Ange Gardien,-
etc. The amendment consists in excluding those townships and municipalities which have been put into the electoral district of Hull, and the rest of the description remains the same. Then, section 9 is as follows:
Number 14 (c), the description of the electoral district of Wright is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:

Then follows the description of the electoral district of Wright as it stands at present in the statute, save that we add to the part excluded North Templeton and the municipality of South Hull. I think that completes the corrections in accordance with the agreement come to with respect to the matter.
In the description of the constituency of Jacques Cartier, the draftsman has put in the wording: " less any part of St. Denis ward." Inasmuch as only a part of St. Denis ward was ever included in Jacques Cartier, and we cannot, therefore, take out the whole, I suggest that perhaps the better way is to make the wording:	" less any
part of St. Denis ward at present included-in said county."
Amendment agreed to.

["When the minister next has his Estimates before the committee he will be expected to give information with respect to the work that Mr. Gobeil, late Deputy Minister of Public Works, has been engaged in for the department.\nAt six o'clock, the House resumed, and then took recess.\nThe House resumed at eight o'clock."]

I do not suppose my hon. friend intends to spend very much this year in negotiating commercial treaties, but we shall be glad if he will give us some information as regards the different agencies that we have at the present time. If I am doing him an injustice in stating that I presume he does not intend to negotiate further commercial treaties this year,
I shall be pleased to correct my statement.

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: This vote is the same as that of last year.
Have you any new agencies since last year?

During the past, year certain changes have taken place, and I will very briefly state what they are. In the first place, our trade commissioner in Germany, who had his head office at Hamburg, was caught and interned, and, although he had some degree of personal liberty, he was obliged to report at frequent stated intervals and was kept under very-close surveillance. He did not succeed in getting out until February, when -a transfer was made with a German consul in South Africa, and he arrived at Rotterdam. As throwing a little light on how close the cordon Is drawn as regards news in Germany, I may say that, although he had considerable liberty and had conversations with a great many people, on his arrival at Rotterdam in February he received his first knowledge that a single Canadian had left Canada and had reached either Great Britain or the Continent. That throws some light on the extreme diligence with which the Germans keep information from getting to such a city as Hamburg. After a little rest, which he needed, he will proceed to Russia. I have made arrangements with Mr. Just under which he is to proceed to Russia by way of the north and spend a three or four months' mission in Russia. He speaks German well, and German is a good deal spoken in certain parts of Russia. He does not understand Russian, but with the aid of English and German, I think he will get through the preliminary work very well. Mr. Just is one of our best trade commissioners; has been well trained; is very diligent and active; understands thoroughly not only how to get information but also how to put it in an illustrative and attractive form. He will enter by Petrograd, and make a tour of Russia, visiting the chief centres and gathering all the information he possibly can. After visiting the western Russian cities, he will take in some of those on the Black sea. He will then proceed through the country to Siberia, coming out at Vladi-vostock, and thence come to Canada by way of the Pacific. Having got all the information he can in that time, I propose to have him spend two or three months in Canada visiting the different centres and having conferences with the boards of trade, business men and manufacturers, bringing to them the information he has gained in Russia, and in that way getting the interests of demand and supply close together. He will then be furnished with two assistants, who will be trade commissioners with him, permanently resident in Russia. Although Rus-122i
sia is much perturbed by the war, yet on account of its vast size and immense population, business goes on in great portions of that territory much as it is usually carried on. When the war is over, we.think that Russia will afford a very large field for certain manufacturers and productions of Canada. Siberia itself is an immense country, much the analogue of our Northwest-quite as extensive, and producing much the same. Siberia has been rapidly filling up with immigrants from western Russia; about six hundred thousand a year are pouring into that portion of the country; and it is on the plans of the Russian Government to develop that country with railways as rapidly as it can possibly be done. So that, both from the east and from the west of Russia, there opens up, I think, a good prospect for our trade. Already some of our manufactures have found a large place in Russia. Agricultural implements to the amount of well on to two millions of dollars were exported to Russia during last, year; and, although that trade is somewhat disturbed at the present time for financial and other reasons, that which has been accomplished shows what there is in the field. Then, a certain section of our manufacturing industries believe that there is a large future there for the marketing of railroad supplies of different kinds, particularly cars, and already some of our manufacturing interests have representatives in Petrograd and are pushing business with their usual diligence.
Mr. Lithgow is .still at Rotterdam. I have kept him there because, although there is not a very great deal of commerce possible now between Holland and ourselves, yet that is a very important situation, and Mr. Lithgow gives us valuable information. He is being retained there for the present.
In China, where they have had a very good trade year, although at present and for some months past the country has been a good deal perturbed, I have appointed a trade commissioner, Dr. Ross, formerly of Belleville, or near there. Dr. Ross has been in China for eight or nine years, connected with business operations. He comes highly recommended. He has been at the work for six or seven months, and fias proved very satisfactory so far as gathering and sending information is concerned, and bids fair to make one of our best commissioners.

In Japan, a trade commissioner was appointed, Mr. Johnson, who succeeded Mr. Harris, and he remained until four or five months ago, when, being an officer in the British army, he felt it his duty to go to the front, and he is now on leave of absence, and is either in Great Britain or at the front, I am not sure which. In the meantime his duties are being performed, and very efficiently performed, hy the commercial attache of the British embassy at Yokohoma, Mr. Orowe, with whom I had the pleasure of making acquaintance. He has been .fifteen or sixteen years in that country, is a thoroughly good commercial man, and, what is more to the purpose, has a very large and sympathetic interest with Canada and its development. For the time being, under an arrangement made with the British Government, he is attending to our work in Japan, and is attending to it 'in every .way satisfactorily.
Two of our young trade commissioners are being trained on the new plan which I explained to the House last year. They were first brought into the department, to be made thoroughly familiar with the methods and purposes uf the department, and drilled in all our work, especially in relation to commerce, and also given some training in customs work, so that they might understand the forms and methods of our customs business. Then they are required to visit different places in Canada and gather information and make reports. The two young men to whom I refer have been with us now for eight or nine months. One of these, I have arranged, is to go with Mr. Just to Russia, to be one of the trade commissioners there under him. The other, in due time, will be transferred to some other position as it becomes vacant.
There has been no change in the trade commissionerships in Great Britain, except that our trade commissioner in Leeds resigned and came to Canada to live. Taking his place and doing his work since that time, has been his assistant, Mr. Dwyer, who is thoroughly well versed in the work of his office and has performed his duties fairly well. It is my intention, in time, to combine two or three of the cities in that district and have them under the charge of one of our trade commission* ers, with a central office and with assistants in the other two centres. I think that in that way, with team work of three men, one at the head, we shall get better results

than with independent commissioners, and shall carry on the work more economically as well.
I think it was stated last year that Mr. Harrison Watson had been appointed trade commissioner in London. He has performed that work satisfactorily. In Australia we have Mr. Ross, who was appointed by the late Government, and who is a thoroughly capable and reliable man-one of the best commissioners we have. In New Zealand Mr. Beddoe is still performing the work. Mr. Pouss-ett is still in South America. Last year, having made a tour of all the states in South America the year before, he came to Canada, went over the country from Vic-, toria to Halifax, and held communications with boards of trade, merchants, and others. He has since returned to his work in South America. Mr. Egan, who was transferred from Manchester, has charge of the work in South Africa, with two assistants. In addition to these services, there is an arrangement by which twenty or thirty British consular establishments are at the service of Canadian trade and correspond regularly with the department, giving information, reports and answers to any inquiries made by ourselves or by merchants or business men of Canada. The service in the British West India Islands is about the same as we had last year. Mr. Watson Griffin was appointed to -make a thorough survey of the British West India Islands, Jamaica and Cuba. This he did; his report is now being published in sections in the weekly trade bulletin, and will subsequently be distributed in convenient form. I think that the business community will find his report very interesting and very useful.

The information which has just been given to the committee by my hon. friend is very satisfactory, particularly with regard to Russia and1 China. There is every reason to believe that soon after the war is over an enormous trade will spring up between Canada and Russia, and I look to the opening up at no distant date of a line of steamers between Prince Rupert and Vladivostock. What my hon. friend has said about Siberia is quite true; we can supply that part of the country with anything they want in the way of agricultural implements. The attention which my hon. friend is giving to the matter ought to bring good fruit in due time.

The lumber industry of the western part of Canada has

been in rather a bad way, and it has not been helped very much by the war, which has disorganized freights and financial conditions. I think the lumber situation in eastern Canada is locking up. Inquiries which are being received from France, Great Britain and Belgium, indicate a 12 noon, more satisfactory condition in respect of certain kinds of lumber produced by Canada. The condition of things in the West during the last year and a half or two years has contributed to a diminution of building activities, and naturally this has had a very material effect upon a large number of the British Columbia mills. Boards of trade and others have been in correspondence with me with reference to some special means by which they could be helped. Trade commissioners in all countries were instructed to make special investigations in regard to markets for British Columbia lumber, and a very extensive and useful series of reports was sent in. Although this information has been useful, British Columbia felt that its case ought to be specially considered, and after mature consideration I acceded to that suggestion as being reasonable, under the circumstances. Accordingly, I appointed a special commissioner, who will take up his duties in a day or two. He will go from British Columbia to Japan, spending a little time there, and will then proceed to make investigations in China and India. China is now a large consumer of lumber, and when she begins to open up and develop her vast resources, lumber will form a most important item of import. What strikes one as he goes through China is the extreme bareness of the whole country. In years gone by, when the principles of conservation were not applied, the timber was stripped from the country, and to-day almost every hill in China is bare to the top. In the northern and far western portions of the country they have, of course, a considerable amount of timber, but the greater part of that vast country, having done nothing in the way of afforestation or reforestration, must depend upon outside countries for its timber. From India, the commissioner will go to Australia and New Zealand; thence to South Africa or South America, I am not sure which; thence to Great Britain, where he will conclude his investigations. I asked the lumber and forests interests in British Columbia to recommend to me a proper man for this position, and they recommended a Mr. McMillan, recently connected with the Forestry
Department in British Columbia, who was born and educated in Ontario, and who has had a good deal of experience in this line.

I wish to call the minister's attention just for a moment to the difficulties of the Maritime Provinces in regard to freight. It is very difficult at the present time to get steamers to carry lumber. The most convenient class of vessels that we now have in Canada is the larger class of schooners, which might very well be employed in the trade between eastern Canada and British Columbia. At the present time there is quite a 'demand on the coast of eastern Canada for British Columbia pine. In the town of New Glasgow where I live, large quantities of it are used in the manufacture of cars for our railways; in fact the specifications in some instances do not permit of any other kind of lumber being used for * certain parts of the car. This lumber has to come by rail, and in many cases at a very great expense. What I wish to point out to the minister is that it could come for half the cost by water, provided that the vessels were permitted to carry it down the western coast of Canada and through the Panama Canal. But the great difficulty is that the coasting laws do not permit a captain holding a coasting license to go into those waters. The laws are now so restrictive that a captain with a coasting license cannot take a ship from an eastern port in Canada through the Panama Canal to British Columbia, or vice versa; and I suppose that nine-tenths of these large schooners that I have spoken of are manned by captains holding coasting, and not deep sea, licenses. If my hon. friend had enough influence with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to get him to remove this difficulty he could do a great deal towards promoting trade between British Columbia and eastern Canada and I think, the eastern ports of the United States as well. That would be a great relief to the shipping people of the Maritime Provinces, who are hampered in their trade not only with the western coast of America, but with South America as well. We are not able to send our vessels down to the River Plate or to Rio or to any of those ports where there is now a profitable business. There is no reason in the world why they should not go there. I think it would be impossible for anyone to furnish a good reason why a captain holding a coasting license should not be allowed to go anywhere

along that coast. Uur captains traded there for a hundred years prior to these new restrictive laws being introduced, and they always succeeded in getting hack and making profitable, voyages. Our captains to-day are just as good men as they were, but' owing to the legislation that has been passed here in regard to coasting voyages they are not able to take advantage of that trade.
There is another question to which I should like to draw the. minister's attention while I am on my feet. Last autumn, after the war broke out, there was eonsider-able discussion in the papers in regard to the prospects of trade in pit props between the ports of Nova Scotia and Great Britain. It was pointed out that owing to the disturbance in Europe the Baltic trade had been cut out, and that the mine owners in Great Britain required large quantities of pit props, and that these might be supplied from Nova Scotia or some other of our Maritime Provinces. A good many people in the Maritime Provinces were interested in that proposal. I am told that my hon. friend has been making some inquiries in regard to it, and 1 am sure that any information he could give to the House and the public as to the prospects of developing a trade in pit props between our ports and Great Britain would be very interesting.
bir GEORGE FOSTER: The matter was taken up by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and a deal of correspondence ensued. It became a matter of very great moment to the mine owners in Great Britain, and they had some conversations with the British Government in regard to it. The result of it all was that a Commission was ajppointel, consisting of representatives of the mine owners and a representative of the British Board of Trade. They came to Canada, and we placed at their disposal all the information and facilities we had. They visited different parts of Canada, taking in Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. They also made a visit to Newfoundland. After they had gathered all their information they made a report which, in the main, followed along this line: the resources wiere ample in Newfoundland and in the portions of Canada that they visited. But some difficulties were apparent. One was the difficulty of freightage, which has been a difficulty in every line of enterprise. Another was that it was impossible for them to lay their hands upon any sufficient supply of 
pit props that were ready for the market. They had then to face this condition: that if contracts were entered into the pit props would have to be cut in Canada during the months of the winter that has just passed, and brought out- for spring and summer transport. Difficulties in two ways cropped up there. No one knew how long the war would last or how soon the Baltic supply would again be accessible-and pit props come from other European countries besides Russia. The trouble then was with making contracts for an indefinite period of time. No one here would like to contract unless he could contract for a year or two years' supply, and the mine owners in Britain did not want to make a contract for one or two years' supply because of the uncertainties of the situation. Some business has taken place; and I think some work has been done during the past winter, but on a somewhat limited scale. The commission also made inquiries in British Columbia, and I believe some busines in pit props has resulted from that part of the country. The commission's report shows that the resources of Canada for the kind of timber have been examined into and found ample. I think that is the main information that I can give my hon. friend.

Is the minister of the
opinion that the trade could profitably be carried on in times of peace?

That will depend. It is thought that the price of pit props will never again be as low as in the past, and if the price is permanently raised it may make business on this side possible. I have also heard that some of the mine owners are substituting metal props for timber, but that is just an experiment, and whether it can be done economically or not I do not know.

In my county a large number of men are engaged in the coal industry. The difficulty in making contracts was that the gentlemen who came to conduct the business in Nova Scotia insisted that the inspection of the pit props should take place on delivery in England. This wood is in itself not very valuable, and our men reasoned this wAy: suppose we send a ship load of pit props which, after a rigid inspection, are condemned; it would be impossible for us to sell that timber, as it is not used for other purposes, and the venture would be a total loss. From the way in which the business is carried on in connection with our mines, of necessity there must be quite a number of

these pit props rejected from time to time by the local people. The consequence is that men in the business fear to engage in any kind of wholesale way in the delivery of these goods to England. If the parties who are interested in obtaining that trade could arrange for an inspection of timber on this side, I am quite sure that there would be a very much larger supply offered. The business of cutting pit props is not confined simply to the winter season in our province but goes on during all seasons of the year. When there is a good deal of snow it is easy to bring this small wood out on sleds, and the opportunity is therefore taken advantage of, but at the same time the work is going on throughout the year. Having some clients who are engaged in this business, I happen to know that this is their principal difficulty with regard to engaging in this business. If the question of inspection was solved there would be a great deal more of this class of timber offered.

It would be quite possible to solve the question of inspection if other conditions could be made right. My own department would be quite willing to undertake to have the inspecting done on this side, and done under specifications as given on the other side, just as we have done in some other particulars. That could be facilitated if the other conditions couia be made right.

If there has been any slackness, that has been the cause of it. You can send deals, or any of the other qualities of lumber that have been going to England, and timber of that class that is found defective in some respects can be disposed of for other purposes, but that condition does not arise in regard to pit props.

The discussion relating to the development of our trade with Russia and Siberia is very interesting to me. I agree with what my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) and my right hon.- friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) have said in regard to the possibility of that trade. For the information of the committee, I might say that about a year ago I travelled with a gentleman from Paris who told me that he, at that time, was arranging to get the capital to put on the North Pacific a line of steamships trading between Vladivostock particularly and our own British Columbia ports. I have no doubt in my mind that the completion of
(the Grand Trunk Pacific will bring to Canada a very large portion of the trade from .Korea, Manchuria and Siberia. It may 'be of interest to the committee to know that, even if this occurred, it would only be a recrudescence of a state of commerce which existed on that coast and between these countries over a hundred years ago. Long before there was a city on the Pacific coast, in California, in Oregon, in Washington, or in our own British Columbia, there was an emporium of Russian trade in the North Pacific at the ancient capital of Alaska known as Sitka. The city of_ Sitka was established in 1799, and 'during the early decades of the last century Sitka was the centre of the Russian trade which supplied the Russian trading posts on the coast and rivers of Alaska and on the Yukon River itself from Behring Sea up the river for a distance of between four hundred and five hundred miles. When the Hudson Bay traders crossed from Hudson bay to the headwaters of the rivers flowing into Behring sea and floated down the Porcupine river on their first trip of discovery, they found, on the lower reaches of the Yukon, the Russian traders there before them. With Alaska, which was then known as Russian America, .and with the coast as far down as the place called Fort Ross, which was within 150 mile-* of the present city of San Francisco, the Russians traded and traded extensively. They bought furs and brought the people engaged in the fur business their supplies. After the transfer of Alaska, or, as it was then called, Russian America, to the United States, which occurred in the same year as our own Confederation, 1867, that trade became practically extinct, and since then there has been very little trade between Alaska, or the North Pacific ports and Russia. However, the trade is there and is capable of being developed in a very extensive way. As a result of the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, the founding of the new city of Prince Rupert, and the establishment of a line of boats from that city to Russian ports, particularly Vladivostock, we shall in a very short time be able to develop a very large and profitable trade.
There is another continent with which I have always felt we have not had as much commerce as we should have had. I refer to the South American continent, and I would like to ask the minister what means we are taking to develop and encourage an interchange of commodities between Canada and that Continent. It is known to the

House that to a very large degree the trade of South America is largely in the hands of European countries-England, Germany, Holland and France. The United States have -not had that trade intercourse with the South American republics that perhaps they might be considered entitled to. It seems to me that the time is opportune for our Government to take cognizance of this fact, and to do everything possible to cultivate commercial relations between Canada and the South American republics, where I am sure there is a great deal of profitable trade to be secured.

Maybe my hon. friend who has just sat down is expecting a word at least in reference to the latter part of his question. I listened, as the committee did, with a great deal of interest to his remarks in reference to Russian trade. The historical reminiscence is a very valuable one, and I hope we shall be able to reproduce the olden trade in much larger proportions. In reference to South America, I stated that one of our Canadian trade commissioners, Mr. Poussett, was instructed, a year and a half ago, to make a complete tour of all the states of the South American continent. He has spent a little more than a year in making a tour of these countries and making a very thorough, and in some respects, minute examination into the conditions of these different states and the possibilities of trade between these states and Canada. His reports have been published widely and supplemented, as I said to the committee a little while ago, by personal visits to different parts of Canada. Mr. Poussett went through our country, spending about four months in visiting all the larger cities. So it remained, and the war intervened. The war, of course, caused dis ocation and difficulties. There is more than simply supplying the demand for the articles to be exchanged in dealing with our trade, or any other country's trade, with South America. There are financial and banking arrangements which seem to be absolutely necessary. At the present time the United States, which has very large resources, which has been very enterprising in reference to South American trade and which has not yet reached a very large measure of success, is up against that difficulty.
It is acknowledged now that what is necessary in order that there may be a remunerative trade and extension of trade between such countries as Canada and the United States and South America, is some form of [Mr. A. Thompson.!
banking and financial arrangement which will put credit and the interchange of money on a fair basis. A great many of these South American states have had to introduce moratoria. They were disappointed in not getting into the European markets, just about the time they were making loans for their own necessities, and they did not get these loans. The state of credit all through South America will take some time to rehabilitate. The' Germans had a system of giving long credits to the merchants, Tunning up to a year and even longer, and that disorganized the business of other countries, and in time led to a large decrease in their trade. But long credits have disadvantages as well as advantages, and in the end I think German trade would have gained no very great advantage. That, however, has been cut clean . across at the present time, and now the' other countries are going in with the idea of not imitating the Germans by giving long credits, and they are trying to arrange banking and financial facilities foi trade. If we are going to do a trade with South America we shall want a direct steamship communication, and that we have not had up to the present. When things begin to settle down, I think this is one of the questions Canada will have to take up.

I found out something which I did not know myself before, and which probably the members of the House did not know, and it is rather an important thing. If you look at the statistics of the production of metals in Canada, you will find that lead, to a certain value, and nickel, to a certain value, are put down as the production of Canada. The fact is, taking nickel for example, if nickel is put down in our returns as having a value of so many millions of dollars, it is the value of the nickel, not as it leaves Canada, but after it has gone out and been refined, and when all the labour and interest on capital, etc., is added to it. It is well for us to have that in mind, and I /think it would also be well in future statistics that this shall be thoroughly noted, so that people may not be led away with the idea that the nickel, lead, etc., that is credited to Canada, is really worth that when it leaves the country.

How is this bounty fund administered, as to when and where the bounty is paid? I do not know what percentage of lead this ore contains, but I believe it is pretty high. For the information of the people in the Yukon interested in that industry, I would be glad if the minister would tell us how this bounty money is paid, whether at the mine or at the smelter or when the lead is smelted.

The object of the bounty was to encourage silver-lead smelting, and the smelting of other ores than silver and gold in Canada, so that it is not a bounty upon the ore but a bounty upon the products smelted in Canada.

Has anything been done by the Government towards prohibiting the export of nickel in its raw state or in the matte?	Canada practically controls the
nickel supply of the world, and there has been a great deal of agitation in the newspapers of late in regard to this question. It was brought up in the Ontario legislature, and I would like to know if this Government has been dealing in any way with the question.

If my hon. friend has been interested in nickel and in the controversy that has been going on, he probably knows as much as I do in regard to that question. We have one of the largest, if not the largest, sources of supply of nickel
in the world, and we are the principal exporter of nickel ore and in the matte-mostly in the matte; but the refining of the ore, as well as the ultimate refining of the matte, has up to the present time been done in Great Britain or in the United States. On account of the uses to which nickel is put, the subject, since the war has broken out, has come to a prominence in another way rather than by the mere establishment of an industry in Canada. The Canadian Government, as I think the House has been informed, has been acting in close sympathy and co-operation with the British Government with reference to the ultimate destination of nickel, and an arrangement has been made between the two Governments, which is entirely to the satisfaction of the British Government, towards directing the ultimate destination of nickel refined from Canadian matte or ore. It is not advisable to say just what that arangement is.

My information is that
the amount of labour expended on nickel after it reaches the stage of matte, in refining it further to make it fit for commerce, is much greater than the amount of labour expended in mining, roasting and smelting, and that absolutely none of the further refining is done in Canada. The whole nickel industry of Canada, which is, I understand, about 85 per cent of the nickel industry of the world, nickel being found in only one other place, namely, New Caledonia, in the region of Australia, is in the hands of two companies-the Mond Company of England, and the Canada Copper Company of Sudbury, which refines all its products in the United States. I do not suggest that the minister should say anything definite at the present time, but serious consideration should be given to the question whether something cannot be accomplished by which the nickel can be refined in Canada or at least within the British Empire. If that were done, we would have a much better control over the industry. If nickel cannot be procured, proper armour-plate cannot be manufactured; so that the subject is worthy of consideration, both from the war point of view and from the economic point of view, of having many millions of dollars spent in Canada instead of in the United States and Great Britain, especially when we have the whole matter in our own hands.

What my hon.
friend says is in many particulars along my own line of thought. I would think, how-

ever, without having made a study of the question, that when you come to the employment of labour, the major part of the labour expended on nickel is done in our country. When you come to the refining of the nickel, a large part of the expenses is on the equipment and machinery; but not being an expert on that matter, I am not certain. My hon. friend is on the same platform with me in this respect, that we are both in favour of inade-in-Canada.

I have received several
petitions asking that the export of nickel be restricted. Possibly the form of the petition emanated originally from the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). At any rate the petitions have been received. While possibly it is not formal, I would be very glad, if the minister would on behalf of the Government, give in a sentence what would be a fair answer to the petitioners.

I do not remember just what the wording of the petition is, but its object is that steps should be taken ii' possible, by which the nickel, which is found in Canada and the initial processes in regard to which are carried out in Canada, should be further refined in Canada itself, so that the finished article being in Canada might be absolutely under the control of Canada, which it is not now, when it is exported either to the United States or Great Britain. The Government, however, while it has a large interest in that question, has not yet come.to any conclusion, either that nickel should be prohibited from going out in the form of matte to another country, or that the Government itself should undertake the operation or refining it. There are a good many factors to be thought of in the establishment of such an industry, and as to the capital and equipment necessary for it in Canada. I do not think I can give any more formal answer than that.

Would the minister make a statement with reference to the amendment made to the Grain Act, which I presume was in response to representations made by the lake carriers in regard to weight on receipt and delivery?

If my hon.
friend has not read the report of the conference with the delegates who visited the Government, I shall be glad to send him a copy. The whole question had its rise in the difficult problem of adjusting the shortages in lake carrying. The shipper puts his grain into the hands of the Government at Fort William, and it goes into the Government elevator or into elevators which are supervised by the Government. The shipper has no power inside of these elevators; his grain is delivered in trust to these warehouse men. When the grain is ordered out of the warehouse it is weighed out by the elevator into the boat, and the shipper has nothing to do with that operation, which is under Government supervision, or under Government management. The weight of the grain that is put in the vessel is therefore given by the Government weighman, and with that grain and that weight the carrier goes on his journey to the eastern elevator. The grain is then weighed out into the eastern elevator, but it is weighed out without Government weighmen and without Government supervision; it is weighed in by the elevator itself into its elevator. If that weight and the weight given at Fort William should agree, there i^ no trouble between the carrier and the elevator, but if the weight given by the in-weighing or receiving elevator is 1,000 bushels short, then, under past conditions, the carrier liad to make up that shortage. The carrier reasoned in this way: that he received from the Government a certain weight of grain at Fort William, that he did not throw it overboard or lose it in any way; but when it was weighed in at the eastern elevator it was short, although he contends that he delivered to the receiving elevator just as much as he got at the loading elevator. Consequently, he demurred against the payment of the shortage. His ground of attack was, that there must be something wrong with the weighing at the loading elevator, or there must be something wrong with the weighing at the unloading elevator. That is the basis of the dispute. The carriers met in convention and came to the conclusion that in this year particularly, having had some heavy losses, and having had all this trouble for years, they would protect themselves by a bill of lading, the essence of which would be that they would not contract with the shipper to make good the shortage, although they would contract to allow a certain percentage as a donation towards this shortage, and
beyond that they would not go. They would not make contracts with the shippers except upon that new or modified bill of lading. The shippers did not accede to that arrangement, and took the ground that they were out of it as far as the lake transit was concerned-that, their grain having been delivered to the Government or Government-supervised elevators, and the grain being weighed out to them, the weight was presumably right, and they should not be held responsible. Therefore they refused to go in with the purpose of that bill of lading. Then, it was thought that if all these people would get together, they might come to some fair arrangement to test out some method by which the shortage could be arranged for each year without the multiplied troubles. It ended in this, that the outloading elevators and the lake carriers were prepared to give contributions towards a shortage fund, to ensure the receiving elevators against losses. If there were any losses greater than this fund made up, then they would stand that part of the shortage themselves. A conference of the carriers and eilevatormen was held lately in my office, and it was pretty representative. Those who were represented there came to an agreement practically on that basis, and I had hopes that the whole thing would have been settled for this year. The idea was to try out that arrangement for one year; if'it worked well, it could be kept on, and if it did not work satisfactorily some other means could be devised. The long and the short of it was that in getting the different representatives from all parts of the country to sign the agreement-the assent of each one was essential to the carrying out of the scheme-delays took place, and I asked them to come together again to see whether we could not come to a final agreement, sign up, and have the whole matter arranged. A number of them came; but it was not a representative meeting. The result is that the situation is about the same as it was before. The question is now engaging the consideration of the officers of my department and of the Government, and before the session closes I hope to bring in an amendment to the ' Act .which will provide some satisfactory way of disposing of shortages, so as to settle the question, if we possibly can, and not have the perennial disputes and troubles and inconveniences which arise from the condition of things that has existed in the past. The shippers, the outloaders and the carriers are agree-

able to haying such an amendment; the objection comes from some of the eastern elevators.
Mr. OLIVER; Has the amending Bill not been put through?

No. I introduced two amendments into the Senate, when I had hopes that this arrangement by agreement would be made as to the shortages. That Bill has come to the House; and, if any further legislation is necessary, as I think it will be, it will be brought in as an amendment to that Bill, so that when it comes before the House, the three questions will be before us, and then the result can be submitted to the Senate and the legislation finished.
As I understood the terms of the Bill that came from the Senate, the question of shortage was put squarely up to the carriers.

There was nothing in the Bill with reference to that directly. The Bill had two amendments, one of which was regarding the certificate of weight at Fort William, as given by the Government weighman. At Fort William you have the shipper and the elevator and the vesselman, and some one has to say what weight is put into a vessel. As the Government system of supervision, if I may so say, seems to be rather better than the system of supervision at other elevators, it was the opinion that the weight ascertained and given by or under the supervision of the Government should be the weight that should be taken as final, and that weight would be put up to the receiving elevator. That would not mean that the receiving elevator would have no recourse after that, but that would settle the weight until, by process of investigation by the grain board, before which the matter could go, or further by the courts, if it went to the courts, an ultimate decision could be had.

As I read the Bill, it seemed to me that if a carrier, having received a certain amount of grain under the supervision of the Government, did not deliver that amount to the receiving elevator, he was absolutely responsible.

He read it, and it was his duty to deliver it to the receiving .elevator. The whole point is that, the Government having fixed the weight, it is supposed to be the proper .weight and the weight which the carrier must deliver. There might be inaccuracies in weighing

the grain at the receiving elevator, and they would have to be determined.

As I understand the
matter, the Government has officials, not only at the Government elevators, but at all the other elevators doing business at the head of the lakes. Does the Government hold itself responsible for the correct or proper delivering of the grain from the time it is weighed in one of the large terminal elevators until it is transmitted into the hold of a vessel? The wheat is weighed in large hoppers; it has then in most cases to be elevated and to go through quite a system of spouts before it gets into the hold of the vessel, and there may be leakage in many ways. When the Government weigher gives a certificate, is he responsible that the amount of grain goes into the vessel, or is he simply giving a certificate that he has weighed a certain amount of grain?

Take the Government elevator first. When grain comes to a Government elevator, it is taken out of the hands of the shipper there. It is weighed out into the elevator, and the Government elevator is responsible for every pound of grain that goes in; it is responsible for delivering an equal quantity of grain both in weight and in grade; if the grain is spirited out of the elevator in any way, that is to the loss of the elevator. The grain remains in the elevator until it is ordered out, and then the Government officials in the elevator weigh it out, spout it out and supervise it as it goes into the hold of the vessel. They have to weigh out just as much as they take in. If they cannot do that, they have to stand that loss. After it once gets into the hold of the vessel the Government is not responsible for what takes place; it is then the carrier's loss.
Mr TURRIFF- That would not cover the point I want to get at. Take the case of a terminal elevator other than the Government elevator. From the information I have received on the subject, I am led to infer that weighers may not be always as correct as they might be. Also that information leads me to point out that discrepancies might occur between the time the wheat is weighed and the 4 p.m. time it arrives in the vessel.

Take the case of such an elevator, and a shipment, say, of 10,000 bushels of wheat, is ordered' out. The 123
Government weigher weighs that wheat and it is sent to the hold of the vessel. But what ,1 am asking is: Does the Government hold itself responsible that it is
10,000	bushels of wheat that is weighed out by their own weigher, or does the Government see to it that every bushel of that 10,000 bushels gets to the hold of the vessel ? 1.	The inspector drops an electric light into the shipping bin, to see that the bin is emptied into the hold.
That is the first thing that is done.
2.	An officer stands on the dock and sees the spouts handled, and shakes them out. The inspectors watch the belts and number the shipping bins for each boat.

If anything goes wr.mg and it is between the weighing-scales and the hold of the vessel, and it is possible for this inspection and supervision to spot it, then, of course, the responsibility falls on the elevator, and they would be made to, as we say, " pony
