Why is it that'while the Government supervise the weighing and delivery of all outgoing grain from the terminal elevators, they do not supervise the transfer of grain from the hold of the vessel to the eastern receiving elevator?

The bent of the department and its administration being towards a proper inspection and certification of grain, as the years have passed by that inspection and certification has been brought to a state of efficiency which, perhaps, we shall not be able to exceed, taking the human element into account. But it is equally important-and, in some cases, more important-that attention should be given to the weighing of the grain, because if the weight is defective the farmer and the shipper may lose large amounts on large transactions. There are difficulties in connection with the weighing of grain. The grain is weighed in, we will say, at a country elevator; then it goes to Winnipeg, and, ultimately, to Fort William, where it comes under the supervision of government weighmen. The scales in all country elevators are under the control of the Inland Revenue Department, and inspection of them, is, therefore, carried out by that department. Up to the present time inspection has been made about once a year, and my hon. friend knows how easy it is for scales to get out of order.

When the Estimates of
the Minister of Inland Revenue were under consideration, I drew his attention pointedly to that condition.

That has been
taken up, to a certain extent, by the two departments concerned. I have no hesitation in saying that it would conduce to the efficiency of the service if both these operations were under the control of one department, that department naturally being the one which has the most to do with the grain. So far, we have not decided to do that, but certain steps have been taken in the matter. In the first place, the Inland Revenue Department has arranged for more frequent and more thorough inspections of the scales in the western division, including the elevators at the terminals. In the second place, we have ourselves obtained from tne Inland Revenue Department authority to inspect and supervise the scales in the terminals at Fort William. The chief weighmaster at
[Sir G. E. Foster.'
this terminal-he	is a	scalemaker,
knows all about scales, and is a very energetic and efficient man-has supervision of all scales at Fort William. The weighing at Fort William has been greatly improved within the last year or two, and, I dare say, is susceptible of staid further improvement. At first attention was directed chiefly to the West, the centre and source of the grain, but gradually it became apparent that something would have to be done in the East as well in order to make the system continuously efficient. Eastern inspection and weighing, particularly the weighing, has not been under the supervision of the Government to the extent that it ought to have been. There is no Government weighing-out from the vessels into the receiving elevator; we do employ weighmen in some eastern elevators who supervise the weighing-out from the receiving elevators into the cars. An Order in Council was passed last year which looked towards bringing the eastern system, in respect of weights particularly, into conformity with the western system. The matter is complicated a little by the fact that the elevator systems of the East differ from those of the West; the Harbour Commissioners have their elevators and manage them, and , it takes a little time to get all these interests in agreement and in accord, so that the system shall be made to work smor.') ly and efficiently all the way through. I hope, however, that before another session of Parliament is held, our efforts in that direction will have resulted in the securing of a more uniform and efficient system.

I cannot understand why there should be many shortages at the eastern elevators. If a vessel has
100,000	bushels of grain for an eastern elevator, exactly that amount is bound to be delivered, and the mate goes up to the weigh scales- and checks the amount very closely in order to establish that the requisite amount of grain has been delivered. You have, therefore, that first check on the part of the vessel owner. In order to avoid dispute between the owner of the vessel and himself, the owner of the elevator also has a man there to check the incoming quantity of grain; that is check No. 2. These elevators, contain a great many bins, the capacity of each bin being from 20,000 to 50,000 bushels of grain, and a cargo of say 100,000 bushels of grain can be placed in two or three bins.
There is in the office-and I know this

from living where there are elevators-a model so to speak which shows exactly the grain of each vessel, and the numbers of the bins in which it is distribued. We will assume that John Brown of Peterborough owns a hundred thousand bushels that came on the steamer Rosedale. That grain is deposited, in bins 1, 2, 3 and 4, we will suppose. The bins may not all be full, but each contains part of the grain. Now when the order comes in to ship that grain it is drawn from the elevator in cars, and it is there that the Government weighman comes in to see that the right quantity goes into the cars. The grain drops out of all elevators from the bottom, and when the four bins are empty that proves that all the grain of John Brown, or whoever it is, has has gone out. If there is not enough grain to fill John Brown's order, the vendor can very speedily get an inquiry into the matter, and unless the grain has been there for a considerable length ot ume the shortage, if any, is easily ascertained. I live where there are elevators, but I do not think there are a great many shortages after all, and some that I have heard of were-say 500 bushels out. That meant that the tallyman had forgotten one tally. Of course the shortage might be only 200 bushels; that depends on the scale. But the grain is very well watched both by the owner of the vessel and the owner of the elevator.

The discussion so far has been largely, 1 imagine, on the outgoing weighing from the terminal elevators. The efforts that have been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce are in the right direction, and I tnink the system is being gradually improved, and that before long it ought to be very complete. There is, however, a considerable amount of complaint about the weighing of wheat at the original elevator where the farmer places it, and at the terminal elevators at the head of the lakes, and possibly the present will be as good a time to discuss this matter as on the amending Bill that my hon. friend is bringing in-. I do not know that I can do better than read a letter on the subject that I have just received, and that seems to me very much to the point. It shows -what the difficulties and the losses are, and gives the writer's opinion how they could best be avoided. The letter is from Mr. D. D. Campbell, Room 246, Grain Exchange^ Winnipeg, Manitoba, and is dated January 13, 1915:
J. G. Tuiriff, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Siir:
I see that It is expected that the Dominion House will soon open for business, and I understand that there are likely to be some changes made in the Grain Act, and it is possible that the Board of Grain Commissioners may be asking for more power to be given them in dealing with matters that may be all right in some cases, but if I had an hour's talk with you I think I could convince you that there never was a time when more definite action is necessary in securing redress from the errors that are continually occurring, especially in weights, both of car lots, and also in cargo lots.	'
The farmers and dealers in the West have far more reason to start a rebellion over the weights they are receiving for their grain than there was for tTTe war which is now raging in Europe. You may say we have the Grain Commission to apply to, and in reply I say we have applied to them, but without results, as the facts which I will state will go to prove. I say without fear of successful contradiction, that conditions never were so bad as they are at the present time, and I have been closely in touch with the grain handling for the past thirty years.
A little over a year ago I took up the work of collecting claims for different grain firms, and also for farmers that desired my assistance, and in that time I have secured adjustments in Weight for the following amounts of grain, by proving to the satisfaction of those in charge that the weights as issued were not correct.
I secured 20,000 pounds of wheat, 10,000 po mds of wheat, 404 bushels of flax, 466.28 bushels of oats, 234 bushels of oats, 95 bushels of flax, 13 6 bushels of wheat, 100 bushels of wheat, 1.3.40 bushels of wheat, 55 bushels of wheat; and I could name a good many more on which I have received adjustments. But sem; of the terminals refuse to make any adjustment, even though the facts are very clear that an error has occurred, hut shield themselves behind the so-called Government weight. And the recent investigations that have been held in regard to cargo lots show*, that some cargoes had thousands of bushels over in weight, and others were found to be short to a large extent.
In fact conditions have got so bad that the railway companies are taking the stand that terminal weights cannot be relied on, and refuse to pay claims for shortages in weight, even where weights have been sworn to as the car was loaded-unless the car has been seen leaking in transit. As an example, I have seven cars which were all handled in about ten days The grain was weighed in by Govern-, ment weight at St. Boniface, and weighed off at Fort William by Government weight; and the shortage on the seven cars is 14,330 pounds. This occurred nearly a year ago, but the claims are not paid yet,
I think the foregoing will clearly show that there is something wrong. What is the remedy? I am prepared to admit that J. G. White, the chief weighmaster at Fort William, is one of the best scale experts in Canada, but I think the facts which I have given show clearly that it is not the scales that cause the errors, but the connections getting the grain

to and from the scales, by the men in charge. Yo i know from practical experience that there is not much to be gained in having good hooks on a chain, unless every link is capable of standing the strain; as the strength of any chain is its weakest link. I claim that we are not paying salaries enough to get men of the right type to take up this work. I claim that there is not a bank manager in Fort William that has any more responsible position than the weighman in one of the large terminal elevators. Note the conditions under which they work and the salaries paid. Is it any wonder that we are not securing accurate weights?
We require a Dominion Utilities Commissioner. with full power to inquire into all troubles arising between the railways and the terjninal elevators, who would have full power to give a ruling- as to where the responsibility rests, and order an adjustment of same. For the average shipper cannot afford to stand a suit in court with a large corporation. I will state a few cases as an example:
A farmer loads 1,100 bushels into a car, and has kept correct record of his weights. The record taken in passing Winnipeg by the Inspection Department goes to show that the car contained the amount claimed. When the car is placed at the elevator for unloading, the record shows that one of the seals on the door of the car is gone, and the outturn of the car is over 100 bushels short. The railway company refuse to pay the claim on the ground that their records show sign of leak or damage in transit, and they claim the car was sealed when placed on the elevator siding. Who is responsible for the loss?
A car is loaded with oats, in Alberta, and consigned to Montreal. This car was first handled by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, as far as Fort William, and taken to Montreal by the Canadian Pacific railway. The outturn shows a loss of nearly $200. Both railways decline any responsibility for the loss on the ground that there was no record of leak while the car was in their possession.
At the time that this car was handled, there was a clause in the Grain Act, as follows: "No grain shall leave a public terminal point without being officially weighed, unless the owner or his agent orders otherwise.".
This car was not weighed, and the Grand Trunk Pacific claim that if it was to be waighed it would be the Canadian Pacific railway that should attend to the weighing, and the Canadian Pacific railway claim that the weighing should have been done by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. This car was handled in 1913 and is not settled yet.
A car of flax loaded in Saskatchewan and consigned to Fort William was noted on arrival at Winnipeg to have been loaded to the wheat line, which is 65 inches high (or supposed to be). On arrival at Fort William the record was taken on two occasions as being 67 inches deep, which is slightly more than thft record taken at Winnipeg. The record shows that this car arrived at destination with \ one of the doors unsealed. The car was unloaded, and the weight given as 61,800 pounds, which is altogether too light a weight for either 65 or 67 inches of flax, and the record of depth is changed to 47 inches by writing a four over the six. The weight sheet shows this car to have been loaded 67 inches deep, and the
[Mr. Turriff.J
Canadian Pacific railway refuse to pay the loss claimed on the ground that the record of the car shows that they delivered the flax to the elevator, and the Elevator Company refuse to make good the loss, on the plea that the record of 47 inches which was arrived at after the car was unloaded is correct. Loss claimed is $429.70.
It is possible that the Board of Grain Commissioners may ask for authority to give a ruling in cases of this kind, but I do not think that it will be consistent, as they would be simply giving a decision on the work done by their own employees, and the last case stated here occurred at the Government elevator, which is operated by the Board of Grain Commissioners. So I think you will see that we require an independent party to decide where the responsibility rests, and whose decision would be final and binding on all concerned.
If it is necessary to secure redress, raise the weighing and inspection charges to $1 for each. That will amount to less than a quarter of a cent per bushel, and if we can secure accuracy by doing so, by all means let us have it.
I presume that will be $1 for each car.
While acting as shippers' agent, I took the ground that we were not paying sufficient salaries to secure the best men. There is twice as much work and three times the responsibility in weighing and inspecting a car as there is in selling it on commission, and at present we pay for weighing 30 cents per car, and 50 cents for inspecting it, and we pay our commission firm, say from $10 to $20, and no one begrudges the commission firm their charge if they look well after the selling of same.
There is no reason why this matter cannot be overcome if it is gone' after in the proper manner.
You will see that this has reference more particularly to the case of dealers and farmers. Dealers are in a much better position than farmers to secure redress for anything that is wrong. In the first place, the railway companies are much more likely to make a fair settlement with a large firm of dealers, or the big millers, than with the individual farmer. In the second place, the dealers and millers are wealthy corporations as a rule, and they are in shape to put up a big fight in the courts if they do not get a fair settlement. On the other hand, a farmer who has suffered a loss of $100, or $400 or $500, is bandied about from one railway company to another, from one elevator company to another, or from an elevator company to a railway company, and under these circumstances, what possible chance has he tc get a fair settlement of his claim? He cannot possibly get a settlement unless he takes the case into court, and there is not one farmer in a hundred who would want to do that. There are very few farmers who would be in a position to do it. It might

cost a good deal more to collect $100 or $200 than the amount collected. This writer suggests that there should be an independent authority appointed to deal with these matter?. It seems to me that there is something in his contention. He mentions eases, and he is prepared to supply the necessary proof in every case, where claims have been outstanding since 1913 and are not settled yet. It seems to me that this is not fair, and if my bon. friend would take this matter up, even now before his amended Bill goes through, something might be done to overcome the difficulties. You will notice that the writer of this letter thinks that it is not the Board of Grain Commissioners who should deal with these matters. There is a good deal of reason in what he says; they would simply be siting in judgment on their own employees. That should not perhaps be given too much weight to, but at the same time there is something in it. A man who would be absolutely independent after all would probably be better able to arrive at what is fair and right than anybody else. I have known the writer of this letter for the last thirty-six years. We settled on adjoining sections in the year 1878, some thirty-six years ago. I have known him intimately ever since, and I am sure my hon. friend the member for Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) will bear me out when I say that D. D. Campbell is as straightforward and as reliable a man as there is in Canada. He is thoroughly well posted in this business, and I would ask the minister to give every possible consideration to the suggestion he makes, and that if possible, when he comes to take up his Bill to amend the Grain Act, he shall do something along the lines suggested, more particularly in the interest of the farmer and of the individual shipper, as he is not in as good a position to look after his own interest as is the grain dealer or miller.

The hon. member who has just spoken was good enough to allow me to see the letter yesterday, and I had an opportunity of reading it over. He has read it to the committee, and it will go upon the record and will be there for further reference and consideration. There are two remarks in the letter which would lead me to think that as good a man as Mr. Campbell is, he is carried away a little by his fervour, -wherein he says that conditions were never as bad as now, and also that they are so bad that
they would be as much a justification for a-rebellion in the West as are the grounds on which the present war is being waged by the Allies against their enemies. This is more, I think, for the purpose of attracting attention than to be regarded as a statement of fact. My officers on the ground and the members of the commission, I think, have at heart the best interests of the farmers of the West in respect to all these things.
There is no doubt about that at all.

They have very carefully watched the matter and have improved methods in every possible way. Their statement to me is that last year showed less grievances and complaints than any preceding year, not only with reference to leakages and weights and certificates and loading platforms and car shortage, but also . in regard to every other thing that comes up as a difficulty in this great transportation system. I should be inclined to take the testimony of men who are every day looking over the whole field, rather than that of my friend who wrote the letter, and who sees, as it were, just a confined area, and has his eye particularly upon his own line of redress of grievances. Consider the human element that enters into it: you have railway systems of tens of thousands of miles stretching from the Rocky Mountains to the Lakes, and on every one of these systems are cars which carry grain, and the cars- may be of wood and other perishable material, and there are good cars and cars that are not so good, and there will be accidents, leakages, and times when the man who breaks the seal and makes inspection forgets to put the seal on again. All these 'things occur, and so long as the human element enters into it, they will occur. It is for us to see that there is the necessary efficient supervision, and we can strengthen the supervision and method by which grievances are to be met and complaints are to be investigated, and we can come to greater perfection, but I do not expect that we will ever arrive at a time in the transportation of grain when everybody will be bereft of a grievance. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) would live in the West fifteen minutes if he did not have some little grievance he could get hold of now and then, in order to keep him alive and quicken his activities.
We do not have to look far for grievances.

I am not finding fault. The Grain Commission, with the full approval of the department, has been bending its energies to the improvement of the weighing system and to the status of the weighmen. The inspecting system has been brought to a very good standard, and now the weighmen have to be looked after. We found the weighmen all temporary employees, with no certainty of how long they would be employed. We found that when the number of men who offered themselves were all combed over to get the best of them for inspectors, the remainder were thought good enough to be weighmen. We have changed that and we are making the weighman a permanent rather than a temporary Officer.
That is good.

The salaries we pay them may not be high, but we have fixed a minimum and a maximum, the minimum being $75 a month and the maxi- [DOT] mum $100 .a month, and if they prove satisfactory their salaries are gradually increased from the minimum to the maximum. They are therefore very much better off than they were before, and we are getting every year a better class of weighmen. Again the human element comes in and mistakes will be made. With reference to these seven cars that went from St. Boniface down to Fort William, I can tell my hon. friend that we might possibly avoid any mistake if at St. Boniface we could see that every grain went into the cars, and if we put a man at the head of the car and another at the taxi of the car, and got them to keep track and watch the sides of the car until it got to Fort William, and then saw that every grain of that get into the elevator was, weighed at Fort William. In that way you would have supervision all the way through and you might come near perfection, but of course that process is impossible. I do not know that the time will ever come when a corporation will pay all claims until it is compelled to, and no man likes to pay until he makes certain that he ought to pay. To remedy these difficulties the writer of the letter says that a man should be appointed who would be an autocrat and a czar, and that when he investigates, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the elevators, have got to do just as he says and make restitution as he declares. It goes a long way to say that the one man shall investigate and pass sentence, and leave no recourse to the

other party for appeal or for courts of law. We have to be pretty careful as to how far we should go in that direction. Our commission could have these complaints made to them and they coidd investigate and they could report, but they have no power to enforce, and it is a pretty grave question as to whether you should give any man or any body of men the absolute right just of themselves to say to other parties what they should do in certain cases, without leaving the other parties any recourse of appeal. I would be glad if it could be made possible that none of these difficulties would occxir, but after all we can only take a comparative view. These are the points that the writer of the letter passes upon, that came within his experience, but count them all up and how few they are in comparison with the innumerable transactions that take place in grain every year in Canada. That does not say that there may be a good many claims that are not brought to the surface, and which would swell that number. It is always a right thing for a minister to say that he will look into the circumstances and that he will take into consideration whatever view is placed before him, and he ought to do it and to do it honestly. If he finds there is anything in a suggestion which car. be practically carried out, it is his duty to try and do it, and he must exercise his judgment in that respect. I know that Mr. Campbell was once in the employ of the Government in this class of business, and his work came ixnder my notice, and so far as his work is concerned I think it was done conscientiously and with a desire to do his whole duty.

If the recommendations which Mr. Campbell makes were carried out, it would cut away his business, so that he cannot be making them from any personal motive. I have every confidence in the way in which the minister is endeavouring to help matters along in that respect, and I have every confidence that he is doing his best to get the law into good shape so that if the farmers do make a loss they will have their remedy. I still think that in the case of the seven cars there ought to be a decision one way or the other long before thi3.

, I quite agree. Of course, as to the management of the interior terminal elevators it is so far an ex-pei'iment. These elevators have a capacity of 3,500,000 bushels of grain storage, and the object is to get the farmers of that part of the country interested in these elevators so


as to study out what possible advantage they may be to them. In order to facilitate that, one of our travelling inspectors, who as regards grain has little to do in the winter months, has been making a tour of the Northwest provinces. He has a nice set of lantern slides which show the construction of the elevators and their workings and give general representations of the mechanical conditions -of the transport system. He calls meetings and exhibits the lantern slides and gives the farmers present an address upon the storage elevators-what they are designed for, what it is proposed to do with them, and in' what way the farmers may make use of them to their own advantage.
I am informed that these meetings are attended with very great interest by large numbers of the farmers. We are also sending out little illustrated pamphlets about the working of our elevators, with the terms, etc., to the farmers of the West, all with the idea of getting the 'farmers to focus their attention upon the Government elevators to see of what use they may be to them. The management is arranging the fees and charges in such a way as to make it an inducement to the farmer to send his grain to the Government elevators. In the arranging of the fees and charges we are for the present absorbing the stop-over charge in the transport system; and, when you take our line of charges, it is possible for the western farmer to put his grain into the storage elevator and have it remain there for 45 days, and then send it forward to our elevator at Fort William and have it transferred to that elevator, all at a total charge which is less than it will cost him to send his grain through the elevators directly to a terminal elevator at Fort William. We think, when that is fully understood, it will have two results. In the first place, [DOT] it will have this best result: it will give an opportunity to the farmer to avail himself of a space of time for the storage of his grain and prevent him from throwing it absolutely and quickly upon the market when it is threshed, because he has no opportunity for storing it. It will thus conduce gradually to the conservation of grain from being rushed on to the market too quickly and sold, thus diminishing the prices which are offered. It offers this inducement also to the farmer, that he can have his grain cleaned and treated and, if it is out of condition, put into condition, all at a comparatively low rate. These are some of the advantages
which we are offering to the farmers in connection with the internal storage elevators.

There is nothing to be
said in condemnation of the idea of the minister to give all publicity possible to whatever advantages there may be in the existence of these internal storage elevators; but the condition remains as it was in the beginning that in the exceptional year the elevators will be used largely, and in the ordinary years they will be used very little, as in the case of the present year as shown by the returns that my hon. friend has given. With three railroad systems operating four tracks to Lake Superior during the summer and three tracks to tide-water during the winter, the conditions which existed some years ago and which were made the original basis of the idea of establishing interior terminal elevators, will have been radically changed; so that whatever reasons there may have been some years ago for the establishment of these storage elevators for storage purposes, those reasons are not now so strong to-day as they were then. I am not finding fault with the Government for establishing the elevators. They will be found to be of use in the exceptional year, but they are not a substitution, nor can they ever be made a substitution in any sense for the original demand made on behalf of the farmers for Governmentjowiiership of all the terminal elevators at Lake Superior.
I wish to say a word in regard to the matter brought up by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). While I want to join the hon. member in what he said as to the minister's good faith in his effort to improve the conditions of the grain trade and of grain transport under the administration of his department, and while I have every confidence in the good intentions of the minister, at the same time I am bound to say that, as I followed his argument, I was reminded of the argument made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) when dealing with the grievances of the lake-carriers and the difficulties of weighing at the receiving elevators. The conditions complained of in the letter that my hon. friend from Assini-boia read is exactly parallel to that complained of by the lake carriers, which has been the cause of serious disputes between the elevator people and the grain shippers, and which is to be made the basis of legislation :by the Government

during this session. The difference is that in the cases brought to the attention of the Government by the hon. member for Assiniboia, the complainant or vi'tim is the individual farmer or the small shipper, whereas in the case of the grain carriers, the complainant is a large organization which has capital and means of bringing what grievances it has to the attention of the Government or indeed of forcing them upon the attention of any government. iSome people say that because it is the individual farmer or small grain shipper who suffers a loss because of leakage or shortage between the interior elevator and the terminals, it is a small matter; but I maintain that, for the success of the Government policy in regard to elevators, it is a more important question than that of the dispute between the carriers and the elevators. If the Government has any purpose in operating the elevator at Fort William, it is to encourage the individual farmer to ship his grain direct, and to give the farmer all the profit that it is possible for him to receive out of the production and marketing of his grain. If the farmer who ships from his local siding either through a local elevator or from an elevated platform, is liable to be robbed of his grain in transit without recourse, then he is certainly going to be deterred from shinninst. And the purpose of the terminal elevator at Fort William is not going to be served. It is not possible to prevent leakages, but it is possible to make the railway company absolutely responsible for any leakages that occur; just as the legislation which is not to be passed, but which is now before Parliament, makes the lake carrier absolutely responsible for any leakage that may occur. When the railway company receives so much grain from the loading platform or the elevator they should turn out that amount of grain at the terminal elevator; and if they lose the grain it should be their loss and not that of the farmer. If the grain is loaded from the platform into the cars, the weight taken at that place, if it is possible to take it, should govern as to the outturn at the other end. That is the object to be achieved, and if it cannot be achieved under present legislation then I think legislation should be provided under which it could be achieved.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman how he would determine 
the weight that goes into the car that is loaded, not at the local elevator but over the platform?
I understand that there is no particular difficulty in weighing the grain into the car from the elevator.

The hon. gentleman was pointing out the difficulty of determining the loss to the farmer who might ship from the local^levator or from the loading platform. If the farmer ships his wheat through the local elevator, he has his weights taken, and has his records. These absolutely determine wnat he has put through the elevator. But if he ships it over the loading platform, there is no way that I know of to determine the weight. I do not j*.now of any way of determining that weight before it gets to the Government weigher at the terminal elevator. That is one of the difficulties the farmer is up against. Loading over the platform, there is no way by which the farmer can determine the weight unless he takes it to a local scale and has each load weigxit^ separately. He has those weights to guide in determining the weight of the whole load in the car, and that might determine it with some measure of accuracy.
I did not quite understand the minister, and while I am on my feet I would like to ask him with regard to a statement he made that a certain time was given to the farmer free who put his grain through the elevators erected at Saskatoon or Moosejaw. But a great deal of the grain of the West is produced at points east of these elevators, and so many of the producers of grain could not make use of them. Would the same length of time be allowed free to the farmer who ships his grain direct to the terminal elevator at Fort William? .
The charge for elevating into the elevators in the West is made low, and the elevating charge covers-storage for a certain number of days.

Does that apply to the
terminal elevator as well as the interior elevators?

For grain that is taken out of the interior elevator and transferred to the elevator at 5 p.m. Fort William the charge is a lower charge, and that carries with it free storage for a certain number of days.
Mr. WRIGHT; The hon. gentleman has not quite answered my question. If the

farmer ships direct to the terminal elevator
at Fort William, what time would he have?
*
Fifteen daysexactly the same as in the other case.

In regard to the point
raised by my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright), certainly if the farmer cannot have a definite weight or measure on shipment, he cannot expect a definite recourse on outturn. But if he can get such a definite weight on shipment, then I say he should have a definite weight on outturn and if he cannot get weight he certainly can get measure. For, when the car is loaded from the loading platform and levelled off, and a chalk line is drawn all around the car at the level of the grain, if, when the car gets to Fort William it is not up to that measure * -that is, allowing for a certain amount of shrinkage- that is proof that there has been leakage. So, the farmer could have a weight, or he could have a measure, beyond any question. There is an instance mentioned by the writer of this letter, of grain actually weighed by the Government weigher at Winnipeg and weighed again by the Government weigher at Fort William, and the shipper had to stand the loss for leakage on the way.

It could not be weighed at Winnipeg. The only way would be to weigh the loads and take what tare may happen to be written on the outside of the car. But the only place where it cau be weighed definitely is at Fort William, or wherever it is unloaded. If the grain were unloaded at Winnipeg, going to a local mill or something of that kind, then the weight at Winnipeg could be accurately ascertained. But the average man shipping his grain to Fort William would have no means of determining the weight of his grain at Winnipeg, outside of taking the cars at their actual tare and deducting that from the gross weight. The weight of the grain is always determined at Fort William; the inspection is done at Winnipeg and Fort William. But there is no way of determining the weight of the grain at Winnipeg.	.

I am not shipping the grain, nor am I handling the elevator; I am simply saying that Mr. Campbell mentioned a certain instance. If I remember his letter correctly, he said that a certain amount of grain, having been weighed at Fort William-*
St. Boniface.

St. Boniface-showed a loss in transit, and that loss had not been made good by the railway company up to date, though the shipment was made nearly a year ago. He urged that there should be some officer appointed by the Government with arbitrary power to make an order in regard to such shortage and enforce the order. Now, I am not going to argue that the Grain Commission itself should not have that power-that this should not be one part of the responsibilities of the Grain Commission. I think the idea of the writer of the letter was that the Grain Commission, being itself in the grain business, so to speak, was not, in all cases, the proper party to render such a decision.
That may be a very fine point, but I think that for the time being most of us would be very glad to give the Grain Commission authority to inquire into and enforce awards in regard to shortages in transit. Above everything else, let the decision be without appeal. In no department of the administration of the law is there greater denial of justice than there is in the unlimited right of appeal. There is no reason why the decision given in the first place should not stand; it is a decision of the human mind anyway, and the chances are that the human mind which had first knowledge of the transaction is the one best qualified to give final decision. So I say that the minister will be well advised if he takes seriously into consideration the complaint voiced by Mr. Campbell, asking for protection to the small shipper in the matter of grain shortages in transit, and that authority be vested in the Grain Commission or in some other body to inquire into and to enforce decisions in regard to the responsibility for these losses. The loss of 100 bushels may, perhaps, be a small thing in a shipment of 150,000,000 bushels of grain, but to the farmer it may mean the loss of his profit on the whole year's work. It is a small thing in the aggregate, but it is a tremendously big thing to him, and his experience will affect the action of a large number of his neighbours. The matter, therefore, has more importance than that assigned to it by the minister. While I give him every credit for good faith in the desire to administer his department well, he will pardon me, as more directly representing the people who are affected by this condition, for pressing their views upon him perhaps somewhat pointedly.

There is no objection to the matter being pressed, but
pOMMONS
I desire to place another view alongside that which has been put forward by my hon. friend. Your man in the West ships a crate of eggs to Winnipeg. He entrusts that shipment to the railway, gets his bill of lading, and the railway has to deliver the goods at the other end. He has a shipment of poultry or crockeryware coming from the east; to all these shipments is applied the common law that regulates the carrying system of this country. All shipments, whether large or small, must be delivered at their destination by the carrier, and if they are not delivered in good form or not delivered at all, recourse is had by the shipper against the carrier. The farmer who deals in grain or in anytning else is subject to the same law; he entrusts his shipment to the carrier; the carrier undertakes to deliver that shipment at its destination, and if he does not deliver it he has to account to the man who ships. It is always the case that the man who ships a dozen eggs is not in as good a position to press his claim as the man who ships a million dozen; the big trader will always have the advantage in making terms or in enforcing his claims against the carrier. That is the common lot of all of us, in every condition of life.

I think that the conditions affecting the grain trade are just a little different from those which apply to the things that the hon. minister has just mentioned. We have a grain commission to handle the grain trade of Western Canada, and if that grain commission are going to handle part of the grain, I think they should handle all of it. If, as Mr. Campbell states, grain was weighed in St. Boniface and again at Fort William or rort Arthur, and a loss of three or four hundred bushels was disclosed, it seems to me that it is plain that the railway company should make good that loss.
We all agree on that.

I do not see why all
-these cases should not be put in the hands of the Grain Commission; as a matter of fact, I think I remember instances in which the Grain Commission interfered in cases of tms kind and succeeded in getting the railway companies to make good the losses that had been sustained. I think that the whole of the grain trade, not merely part of it, should be put in the hands of the Grain Commission.

I have listened with
a great deal of interest to the addresses, delivered this afternoon; particularly am I interested in the paternal solicitude which is exercised by the Government and by the minister over the farmers of the West. Great care is taken that everything is done for the western farmer; with the eaestern farmer it is quite different. I should like to know what is the quid pro quo for the miner and the fisherman and the lumberman in New Brunswick,. Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island who pay their fair share of all this money that is being expended in the West? I remember that as far back as 1881 we started to put our money into the West for the development of the land and of railways, and so forth, and we have been continually doing it ever since. And now we are spending our money in paying commissioners and other officials to see that the farmer of the West is protected. T7je story in the East' has always been that we should give for the purpose of developing the West, so that it might become the granary of the world, that foodstuffs would become cheaper by reason of the enormous amount of money we were spending in the West, and that flour, which thirty years ago was dear in the Maritime Provinces, would certainly become cheaper. But after twenty-five or thirty years' experience we find that flour instead of getting cheaper is getting dearer. In fact, I 'do not remember any time when flour was as dear in Eastern Canada as it is to-day. If any miner, in my part of the country who is paying $9 or $9.50 a barrel for flour asks me what has become of all the money that he contributed in the way of duties on flour and woollen goods and almost everything that he and his family uses, I am not in a position to tell him. But we pay commissioners and ministers and others to get this information, and I hope the minister this afternoon will be able to put on Hansard something that I can tell the lumbermen and miners of N'ova Scotia when they ask me what has become of their money and how it is that flour is getting 'dearer in stead of cheaper. I wish the minister and the Government would show some solicitude and following care, if I may so call it, over the grain till it becomes flour, and after it becomes flour till it gets into the store and is sold to the miner and the fisherman who has no middleman at all, but has to depend on his own capacity to make the best bargain possible. It looks to me as if there was

some combination of millers or Hour merchants who are putting up unnecessarily the price of flour. This discussion came up in the House a few weeks ago on a motion of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) that there should be some control over these prices. It is a difficult matter of course. But we have a Railway Commission in this country, and the origin and the principle of the formation of that commission was to ha've some control over freight rates. That Commission became necessary aftef twenty or thirty years of experience in this country. Why, then, should there not be some control over the price of flour? There may be a difficulty in doing it, but all the.greater necessity for dealing with it; and I believe the day will come when it will be necessary to have a Commission in this country to deal with the question of the prices of flour and all the other commodities that the people must h ave.
May I ask whether there was any complaint about the high price of flour l efore the war? My impression is that the price of flour was not very high in Canada before the war began.

Oh, yes. For the last two years in our part of the country the price of flour has been gradually rising, and for at least nine months or a year before the war there was a very strong cry in our part of the country that t.ie price of flour was inordinately high. Yet we are told here that there is an abundance of wheat in the country, more than we can hope to sell to the people who are very much affected by the war. xind that being the case, I am afraid that this cry of the war is simply made the occasion for millers and others to put up the price. If we have more wheat than we can export, if we have plenty of mills and plenty of wheat, I do not see that the mere fact of war should be an excuse or a reason for inordinatly putting up the prices. What I wanted to submit to the minister was that when the fisherman in Nova Scotia has fish to sell he must look after it himself. He must find a .market for himself, and if any of it is lost in transit he has to find his way through the courts as -best he can. There is no commission or machinery of any kind whatever to help the fisherman in selling his goods, and the same with the lumberman and the miner. They have contributed money in large amounts towarus the development of the West, but they have to look out for
themselves the best way they can. We are all glad that the West is developing, but I am not making a far-fetched argument when I say that the contention in Eastern Canada always was, as the minister knows, that the day would come when the enormous development of the West would give us cheap flour, cheap foodstuffs, and so forth. I say that there should be strong oversight at all events, over the grain from the time it leaves the farmer until it is put in the flour barrel, and after it is put in the flour barrel, until it is sold to the miner or the lumberman or the fisherman, who must buy it at the price it is offered. If the machinery of the minister's department is not sufficient to supervise these matters, the people are willing to pay for any further instruments that he may bring to his aid in keeping these things right. At all events we hope and expect him to be in a position to tell the people of this country that the prices are too high. Even if he does not interfere with any machinery, by way of a commission or otherwise, he should tell the people that the prices are too high, and then it would be time to see whether or not there was a combination and the proper remedy to apply.

Do the fishermen of the
province of Nova Scotia use western flour in the pure state, without blending?
Yes, there is no other flour for them to buy.

I do not propose to follow up by way of answer the sectional appeal made by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). I do not propose to follow up his complaint that this Government is too solicitous of the good of the western farmer. I am very proud to say they have been solicitous, but I refer his complaint to better hands. I leave it to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and I know they will reply to it in much more forceful language than I could use. I am also hopeful that their appeal to him will have more effect than any I could make. Perhaps I could suggest to the hon. member tnat we pay out annual bounties from the treasury to the fishermen, about one-half of whom I think are in the hon. gentleman's own province. We are very glad to pay those bounties, and none of us grudge them in the least, but there is no corresponding bounty in connection wiui any other industry in our country.
Does the hon. gentleman know the origin of those bounties?
I am quite aware that they are paid out of the revenue from an award which was made by a tribunal.
It is Yankee money.

That award, when it
was made, was the property of the whole Canadian people, and if any had a particular interest in it, it would be the fishermen of earlier days, and not the fishermen of subsequent times. However, that question does not arise, because no one for the purposes of this debate questions the propriety of it at all. What I rose to say was this: The hon. member for Edmonton has offered some observations on the advisability of the Grain Commission having the control and disposition of shortages and overages arising chiefly through carriage by water, and to some extent also through carriage on land.
He has argued that it would be well were the grain commission given power to fix responsibility and assess the proportion in which the shortages should be borne. On the other hand, my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce argues that that would be departing from the general scheme of fixing responsibilities, and that dealers in western grain have no more right to appeal to another tribunal in respect to grain than they would have in respect to other commodities or than citizens in other parts of Canada would have in respect to articles they shipped. I wish to offer another suggestion to lay alongside of the -two. It is, I must admit, in support in some degree of what has been advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton. The question of a tribunal to which any traffic must be referred is after all simply a question of which tribunal is best. If it were possible, for any other class of damages, or any other class of difficulties, in regard to civil rights, or the regulation of the trade, to establish a tribunal other than the courts which would give better results than the courts, in my opinion the people engaged in that trade would have the right were the class large enough to that tribunal. The whole question amounts to this: is the class of cases of such extent, and do these cases involve such special matters of investigation and difficulty, that a special tribunal can best deal with them? It is well known that very many problems are now referred not to the courts but to commissioners. The province of Ontario now 
presents a most pronounced example in connection with the administration of a very large area of cases-cases in connection with workmen's compensation. They have relieved the courts entirely of the disposition of these cases and committed them without recourse to a workmen's compensation commission. The question as to whether in this case reference to a commission would be the better method I would think, would be this: is that commission in a better position than any court to dispose of questions of shortage and overage and to make regulations in the main governing the disposition of shortage and overage? Is it in a better position to do that? If it is, it appears to me that the question is settled. If it is able better to get at the evidence, if it is composed of men more familiar with the trade, if it is provided with the means of getting the evidence and doing substantial justice, to a greater degree than the courts, then, it appears to me, we have the answer to the problem, and such a tribunal should be clothed with the necessary powers. May I put it again? The question before us is not: are the people entitled to any better remedy than any other? They are entitled to the best they can get. If the Grain Commission is the best tribunal, then we should give them the Grain Commission. It appears to me that it is the best tribunal because it appears to me that in the long run likely more justice can be done than by recourse' to the courts. The main reason is that in this matter of the regulation of the traffic in grain there might in the courts be great delay. Delay is exceptionally dangerous, and delay is inseparably incident to court procedure. It might be better that the usual rules of evidence should be departed from, and perhaps injury done in some cases, than that we should be compelled to resort to the protracted proceedings of the courts.
I offer this only alongside of the views put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton.

It seems to me that
this discussion is founded upon what may be called the fallibility of the human race in regard to its own affairs. The various sufferings which people endure by reason of their incapacity are made up for as nearly as possible by what is known as a system of insurance. It is possible, therefore, where people cannot have recourse to law, or because the facts are such that they cannot be reasonably ascertained, to institute a system of insurance so that there will not really be any injustice done to any-

body, and this system might reasonably be extended to all Canada. Perhaps we could go a little further and extend it to every branch of that trade. We have had the same principle worked out after a great struggle during a long course of years in the Workmen's Compensation Act; let us have it also here. I do not think it is quite fair to say, as the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) has said, that we are spoon-feeding the West all the time and that we get no return. I must confess that I am a little frightened at the present time, considering that the farmers of Ontario, by reason of the decrease in the price of their farms through the competition of the West, have lost not less than $500,000,000 for the benefit of the West. But I wish to emphasize it, and I believe I am right when I say, that this difficulty could be overcome by means of the institution of an insurance policy. It seems to be quite reasonable and proper that the Government should institute it. They might possibly assess the shipper and the producer everywhere a very small amount for that purpose. There is no real reason why the state, which undertakes to control and administer the affairs of the people, should not provide in every particular for the efficient carrying out of the same.

I would like to ask the
minister if he would give the committee any explanation of the increase in the price of flour. The minister has described the care that is taken of the farmer's wheat from the time it leaves the wheat fields until it arrives at Port Arthur. After the grain has reached that point, what action, if any, does the Government take? Does the Government's action cease at Port Arthur and does the minister know why the price of flour has increased during the last few years? What happens after the wheat has reached Port Arthur and is put on board the boat there? Is there any other control exercised over the shipper, the carrier, the miller or the middleman before the flour finally gets to the consumer?

It is somewhat cruel of my hon. friend, when my attention is centered on this great elevator and grain business, to call me back to a problem which we could discuss for a long, long while. I might at least give my hon. friend one reason why flour is higher
to-day than it was two years ago: it is because the price of the grain out of which the flour is manufactured is a good deal higher than it was.
I remember that three years ago good merchantable wheat out of which good flour could be made, could be bought in the West at from 55 cents to 65 cents per bushel, but at present you cannot buy that same wheat for less than from $1.35 to $1.50 per bushel. The fundamental cause of the increase in price is the war and the conditions that have arisen from the war. I think you will find it true if you take all commercial transactions into account, that the moment there is one very predominating cause that makes for a rise in the price of an article, there is a tendency to give that a boost by everybody who has something to do with the handling of that article. I think myself that in the stores of Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, we are paying to-day higher prices than are warranted by intrinsic conditions, simply because of the rise that has taken place in the staple commodities because of the war, and, in sympathy with that there is a tendency for everything to go a little higher. That is somewhat unphilosophical, but I think it may explain a little bit of the rise. The main reason is due to the fact that the material out of which flour is made has almost doubled in value, and there is beyond this a period when no man knows to what prices may go, and under such circumstances there is a tendency not to reduce prices, but to hold on and keep the prices up. I hope my hon. friend will excuse me for not going further into this.
The minister has expressed the view generally held and I am thankful to him. What supervision is exercised after the grain leaves Port Arthur?

Mr. MARC1L: What is the policy followed by the minister in regard to promotions in the inside service? Did the minister ask for applications for the position of chief architect, or did he ask only this particular man to fill the position?	[DOT]
We had been looking for some months to get a man to take this position, before we decided upon Mr. Horwood.
Did the Civil Service Commission advertise for a chief architect?

Why was not the appointment made through the Civil Service Commission? I understand that all the appointments in the different departments are filled through the Civil Service Commission; that is, a department asks the Civil Service Commission to recommend a man, and the commission advertises in the Canada Gazette and posts up advertisements in the different post offices throughout tne country. The minister does not know whether or not he could have got a man for less than $7,000. If Mr. Ewart's salary was $4,000, there is an increase of $3,000, although the cost of living has not increased in that proportion. I find fault that in the different-departments the ministers are too prone to pay very large salaries to the chief officials and to let the poor messengers starve on $500 a year. A messenger came to me the other day and said that he had been in the hospital. He had to go into the public ward; and when, the bill was sent to the city, the city would not pay it, the city treasurer claiming that the Government should pay their men sufficient salaries to enable them to pay their hospital bills. This man said that his wife had been sick, and that he could not afford to call in a doctor. Rents are very high and the cost of living has increased. The minister goes on increasing the salaries of the higher officials from $5,000 to $6,000 or $7,000; in fact, the salary of the Deputy Minister of Justice was increased to $10,000; yet poor messengers who have families to support receive only $500 per year.

It is one of the weaknesses of the Civil Service Act that the minimum

salary to start with is $500 a year. We cannot pay more.
The minister should be solicitous for those poor people, and not too solicitous for those who have high salaries.
I quite agree with my hon. friend.

The minister might have been able to get a good architect for the salary that Mr. Ewart was receiving/or at least for $6,000 a year. It is an important position, and the minister should have asked for applications and not have selected only one particular man, because he happened to have connections in Winnipeg and to be a friend of my hon. friend.

I suppose I will not be accused of being disposed with undue favour towards the members of the ministry or towards the Minister of Public Works; but it strikes me as hardly seemly that an officer of the 'department should be on the same basis as regards salary as the minister who is in charge of the department and whose responsibility must necessarily be very much greater. Either the minister should have more or the employee should have less. In the present time of stringency, it would appear that the alternative would be that in no case should an officer be at as high a salary as the minister. If a special technical employee must receive a high salary, surely the man who is responsible for the discharge by that official of his duty should in common sense receive proportionately more or at least enough to make a distinction between the two positions.

I quite agree with my hon. friend. Of course, the salaries of the ministers should be much higher than they are. At the same time, my hon. friend will understand it is impossible to get a chief architect or a chief engineer to-day who is not already in the department at any salary below the amount named. There is no respectable architect in business in any part of Canada that does not earn more than $7,000 in his own office. It would be impossible to get any architect suitable for the important position of chief architect of the Department of Public Works at any less salary than $7,000.

It seems to me there is great objection from another standpoint- that the minister has gone outside of his department to select a chief architect. For

the proper encouragement of the men in the different departments, the principle of promotion should be acted upon. In the department, I know-I do not think I can possibly be mistaken-there are men, or were when I was minister, who are thoroughly qualified to take the position of chief architect. I have not a shadow of doubt about that. I think it is very objectionable to go outside and bring in a man and place him over the heads of those who have been for a long time in the department, and give him a greatly increased salary. This Government seems to be trying to break the Civil Service Act all to pieces, and I do not know of any more glaring case than the present. Take the chief engineer: he is well qualified to discharge his duty, and yet he receives a salary of only $4,000. That, I think, was fixed by the Civil Service Act by unanimous consent of this House. His duties are more onerous than those of the chief architect. They certainly require as great ability and qs good judgment for their proper discharge. The chief engineer has been for a long time in the department, and, as I have said, he receives a salary of $4,000, in accordance with the terms of the Civil Service Act. Yet a new man is brought in and placed over the heads of all others, at a salary nearly double that which the chief engineer receives. It does seem to me that my hon. friend is making a great mistake in doing this. He is taking a step calculated to create discontent in the department, and is violating in the strongest way, not only the terms but the spirit of the Civil Service Act.

I agree with a great deal of what my hon. friend has said; but we had to deal with the case on practical considerations. The occasion for the appointment of the new chief architect was that Mr. Ewart asked to be relieved of the heavy responsibilities. The only other man that I know of who was in the department and who could have taken the place of Mr. Ewart as chief architect, was Mr. Wright. But Mr. Wright conceived the idea that he could do a much better business for himself outside the department, and resigned a short time before Mr. Ewart did. Had Mr. Wright still been in the department, he would undoubtedly have got the position of chief architect, because he is a really good man. But, after Mr. Wright, there was no one in the department who aspired to the position of chief.
What was Mr. Wrights salary when he resigned?

It was $3,800. He was a very good man; he had the material in him for a chief architect had he not resigned. It was necessary in the public interest to engage a good chief architect, and it is impossible-or was at that time- to secure one who would fill the position at less salary. This salary was approved by the House and voted last year.
The sailary of $7,000 was not. voted?
Yes.
Why is the vote of $3,000 in the Supplementary Estimates this year?
Because the chief architect was not appointed until six months ago. We had to put his name in the Estimates by reason of the fact that he has not passed the Civil Service Commission.
It being in violation of the Civil Service Act, he has to be named?

When the minister next has his Estimates before the committee he will be expected to give information with respect to the work that Mr. Gobeil, late Deputy Minister of Public Works, has been engaged in for the department.
