On March 5, I asked the following questions of the Minister of Public Works:
1.	When did A. Gobeil retire from the posi-stion of Deputy Minister of Public Works?
2.	How long was he in that office?
3.	What was the amount of his retiring allowance under the statute?
4.	Is he employed by any department of the Government at the present time, and what is the nature of such employment?
5.	What is the total amount he receives from the Government at the present time?
The following answers weie given:
1.	1st July, 1908.
2.	Appointed deputy minister on 1st January, 1891.
3.	$2,160.
4.	No.
5.	$2,160.
I felt that there was something which the Minister of Public Works had not given out in his reply to these questions, so subsequently I addressed the following questions to him:
1.	Was A. Gobeil, former Deputy Minister of Public Works, employed by any department of the Government since October 10, 1911?
2.	If so, what was the nature of such employment?
3.	What was the salary or remuneration paid him in respect of such employment?
4.	When did such employment cease?
And this is the answer I got:
1.	Yes, from 15th June, 1912.
2.	To prepare a complete history of the port of Quebec, in relation to the St. Lawrence trade; to investigate titles of ownership of lands required in connection with St. Charles river improvements, and compile other information required by the department.
3.	The difference between his superannuation allowance, $2,160, and $5,000, the salary of a deputy minister.
4.	January 31, 1915.
These replies reveal a most extraordinary condition of affairs. Mr. Gobeil retired in 1908, after having discharged the duties of deputy minister since 1891. On the 15th of June his salary was restored to $5,000, the salary pertaining to the office of Deputy Minister. When I addressed the question to the Minister of Public Works on the 5th day of March, it anticiliated by a few days the. date upon which Mr. Gobeil's salary cheque for the month of February would have gone out; for I understand it is the rule in the depart-

ments-I am familiar at all events with the Department of Railways and Canals-that the salary cheques go out on the 10th of each month. When I asked the question of the minister on the 5th of March, the February cheque had not gone out, and would not have gone out for a few days in the ordinary course of events. Then Mr. Gobeil's employment with the Government suddenly terminated. The employment given to him was of an extremely indefinite character. According to the information given by the Minister of Public Works it would appear that on the 15th of June or some time previous Mr. Gobeil came to the department and saw the then Acting Minister of Public Works, and that as a result of their interview it was decided that Mr. Gobeil's salary would be restored to $5,000. Mr. Gobeil's services commenced on the 15th of June, 1912. Between that date and January 31, 1915, he has drawn, in addition to his superannuation allowance of $2,160, no less a sum than $7,457. I should like the Minister of Public Works to be good enough to say whether or not the work entrusted to Mr. Gobeil, as indicated by his reply to my question, is complete. .

In answer to my hon
friend, I would say that what he states is correct. In view of the fact that Mr. Gobeil had such a general knowledge of the public works of this country, and in view of the necessity for an examination in connection with the contemplated work at the harbour of Quebec and in the St. Lawrence river, it was evidently thought by my predecessor in office . that Mr. Gobeil would be a suitable person to make a report on the situation. He was therefore employed and he carried on the work with a great deal ot vigour. On the 31st of January last we felt that the services he had rendered were such as to complete the work he had in hand, and he was therefore relieved of any further duties in connection with reporting on the matter of the development of the harbour at Quebec and St. Lawrence river. These are the facts as closely as I can carry them in my mind. It is true that Mr. Gobeil was employed for the time mentioned by my hon. friend, but, as I said, he is no longer an employee of the department.

Has the minister a copy of this opus magnum to which Mr. Gobeil

has been devoting his time since the 15th of June, 1912?
I have noit a copy here. I shall be glad to find out whether there is a copy in the department and let my hon. friend see it if he wishes.
Has the book been published yet?
Not yet. It is a report, not a book.
It says that he was employed to prepare a complete history of the port of Quebec. Has the copy reached the hands of the publishers yet?
Not that I am aware of.
Who is to pay for publishing this work ?
I do not know that it will be published at all. It will be simply a history of the port of Quebec, for the information of the department.

Has the department the
history yet?
Not that I am aware of.
Then the department has nothing yet for this $7,457?
We have the benefit of all the information that Mr. Gobeil has in connection with that work. I understand the report is being prepared.
The minister has not the benefit of all the knowledge Mr. Gobeil has, because he has not received the report yet. When does the minister expect to receive it?	*
Very shortly.
Is this course being pursued with regard to the Harbour Commissioners in other parts of Canada?

Mr. Gobeil had nothing
at all to do with the Harbour Commissioners in the city of Quebec
Has the Government undertaken the preparation of a history of any of the other harbours of Canada?
Not that I am aware of.

So this special employment
that was given to Mr. Gobeil was without a precedent?
Is it intended that this work shall be distributed throughout Canada, or is it just for the benefit of the department?'
Wherever there is a necessity for it.

What were the terms upon
which Mr. Gobeil was employed?

All the information the
department has is in the answer given to my hon. friend's question.

Well, the department has
not very much information. It is rather an extraordinary coincidence that when Mr. Gobeil was employed to do this work there was no remuneration fixed except that he was to enjoy a salary, in addition to his superannuation allowance, which would bring his income up to the sum of $5,000. It is perfectly clear from the statement made by the minister that there was no agreement or contract under which any special work was to be done, but that Mr. Gobeil was for all time, so far as the present Government is concerned, to get around the Superannuation Act and enjoy the salary of $5,000 just as if he were a deputy minister. The minister says that on January 31, Mr. Gobeil's work having been completed, his services were discontinued. Now the minister does not know whether his work has been completed or not, because he has not a copy of the manuscript that Mr. Gobeil prepared, if he prepared anything at all. I should think that if Mr. Gobeil had any legitimate or proper employment it should not cease until his work was in the hands of the minister, and the minister would be able to pass upon the question whether that work fairly represented the amount of money that, was paid. I am bound to s^ay that the sum of $7,457 is a pretty tidy sum to be paid to Mr. Gobeil in addition to his superannuation allowance for the preparation of a history of the port of Quebec. If the question had not been put upon the Order Paper I venture to say that Air. Gobeil would still be enjoying the emoluments pertaining to the employment given to him by the late Minister of Pub-lie Works. The fact that this employ-

ment was given to him by the late minister does not exonerate the present minister from some responsibility. I say that under the circumstances there is no justification for this expenditure of money. The minister admits himself that he knows nothing about the work or the manner in which it was carried on, and he does not know at the present moment whether the work has been completed. I stated before that it was only after my question had been placed on the order paper that Mr. Gobeil's employment terminated. If I had not put the question when I did the presumption is that Mr. Gobeil would have continued to enjoy the emoluments pertaining to the particular employment in which he was engaged.
It is a significant fact that no special compensation was allowed to Mr. Gobeil, but he was to get such a sum as would make up the difference between his superannuation, allowance of $2,160 and $5,000. This is only another way of getting around the Superannuation Act by which a friend of the Government was able to draw from the treasury of this country the sum of $7,457 for services of the value of which to the Department of Public Works there is no evidence.

What was really the object of this gentleman going down there and writing the history of the port of Quebec? Is the information not really contained in other histories? How has the Government or the country been able to benefit from a history of the port of Quebec? Was it to help to promote any trade interest or development? Along what line was it necessary that this man should be sent down to do such a thing as that? Was it absolutely necessary to write a history of the port of Quebec to promote ally material interest in connection with that port?
Is the report published?

No; we have not received it yet. I might say in answer to my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that the port of Quebec is an especially important port and one that requires a great deal of consideration at the hands of the Government. My predecessor, Mr. Monk, was very wise indeed in employing the services of one so capable to deal with the work of research which Mr. Gobeil undertook to do in connection with the port of Quebec. It was contemplated at that time, as is evidenced from the amount of money that has been spent during the past three years, that great development should take

place in that particular port. It was undoubtedly advisable in the public interest that we should have all the information for our use which it was possible to obtain and which we have had both by personal correspondence and conversation with Mr. Gobeil from that time on. Now that he has succeeded in gathering all the information at that port, he is no longer in the employ of the department and his report is expected daily. When it comes I am sure that the report will be of great value and great interest not only to the people of Quebec but to the people in different parts of Canada generally who take an interest in the development of our national ports. There are few, if any, ports that are more important than the port of Quebec, especially in view of the fact that we are about to establish a large dry dock in that port, that large docks are to be constructed and that the harbour commissioners are about to expend large sums of money in the erection of an elevator and other important works. In view of these things it was in the public interest that my predecessor should get the best information and with that object in view he evidently employed Mr. Gobeil.

I do not understand just what the minister means by his statement in answer to my question. The port of Quebec is to be an important port, a dry dock is to be established, elevators are to be built, many other things are to be done, but the mill does not grind with the water that has gone through. To me, an ordinary onlooker, it would certainly seem unnecessary that Mr. Gobeil should go to Quebec and report on what the port of Quebec was one hundred years ago. It would not help to build elevators or dry docks or show what ought to be done in the future. I quite sympathize with the minister in doing the best he can for his predecessor, but I believe that if he looks this matter squarely in the face, as he and I, ordinary business men, would, he will agree with me when I say that we would not waste more than a couple of hours in reading aboht what the port of Quebec was a hundred years ago, for the purpose of helping us to do something in connection with that port to-day. I am still at a loss to understand why Mr. Monk should have sent Mr. Gobeil down to make a report on the history of Quebec. Take the very important and flourishing port of Sarnia; we might have a history of that port written for the last hundred years, and possibly if we were real good, and wrote and published

the history of Sarnia, we might have elevators, a drydoek and other things there.
I doubt very much if the minister would accede to a request to send a man to write - a history of the port of Sarnia. In all seriousness, I quite appreciate what the minister has said, but again I ask, wherein do the people of Canada benefit by the fact that he has got an unpublished history of Quebec for the past seventy or eighty years.

My hon. friend uses the word "history" of Quebec. That may be the term that was used in some of the correspondence, and he may be correct from that point of view, but, as I understand Mr. Gobeil's appointment, it was in connection with the practical work about to be undertaken in that port. The unhappy phrase "history" of Quebec might have been used, but it was not intended that he should write a history of Quebec in the ordinary sense of that word.
Has not the harbour commission of the port of Quebec an engineer to look after its work?
Mr. Gobeil ~was appointed before the harbour commissioners were appointed.
Is there an engineer in the employ of the harbour commission?
Yes.
Is it a fact that Sir William Price, chairman of the harbour commission, has resigned?
We were so informed to-day.
Has the resignation of Sir William Price been accepted by the ministers?	'
It has not been accepted yet.

I would like to ask the minister if Mr. Gobeil has not been employed also in making valuations of land on the St. Charles river in connection with the locks to be constructed at the mouth of that river? Is there a report in the hands of the hon. gentleman as regards the cost of the locks, and also the cost of the expropriation in connection with the riparian rights?

My hon. friend is quite right, and I overlooked the point in referring to the matter that Mr. Gobeil had made reports to the department in connection with the proposed works now under
way on the St. Charles. We have these reports, and I will be glad to bring them down to the House.
What is the approximate cost of the proposed expropriations on the St. Charles river, as reported on by Mr. Gobeil?

As far as my memory serves me, the value placed by Mr. Gobeil upon the land to be expropriated is something like $600,000. The price at which the land was valued was 23 cents a foot, and the value of another portion was fixed at a higher figure than that. The smaller portion, which was at the higher price, we refused to accept, but last year the owners came down to the price of 23 cents for the piece at the higher valuation,' and we accepted it.
As I understand it, the owners are now prepared to accept the twenty-three cents, but as the result of a further valuation we think our previous offer was too high, and it will likely go to the Exchequer Court.

I wish the minister would submit to us at the next sitting of the House, a copy of Mr. Gobeil's report on the expropriation of those riparian lands on the river St. Charles, and also a copy of the plan showing where the expropriations will take place.
We have such a plan and report and I shall bring it down.
Will Mr. Gobeil receive any remuneration for the work to which my hon. friend has referred?

No, that was part of the work to be done for his salary.
Mr. IiYTE: Has the minister correspondence with Mr. Gobeil, defining the work he is to do for this salary and giving the terms of his engagement?
My deputy informs me that there is simply a letter written in 1912 from the chief engineer to Mr. Gobeil.
Will the minister bring that down?
I shall be glad to do so.

How does the minister explain that Mr. Gobeil's remuneration was fixed at the difference between $2,140 and $5,000? Is that the usual terms upon which legal or other services are engaged by the department?

The remuneration was fixed at the sum which the then minister

thought fair and reasonable. The Superannuation Act provides for a man being brought back at the same salary he had previously received, and probably that was in the mind of the minister when he fixed the sum at $5,000.
Is there anything in the correspondence to indicate when Mr. Gobeil's work was to be finished, or was it to be a continuous engagement during the life of Mr. Gobeil?
I have not read the correspondence, but I will bring it down and the hon. member can read it. Mr. Gobeil is not in the service of the Government at the present time.

I understand that, but it
might be well for the minister himself to read the corresponderfce.

speechtext:
The only reason why Sir
William Price handed in his resignation is, that he being a man with large interests finds it difficult to give to the discharge of the duties of his office the time and attention required. It took Mr. Gobeil a long time to write his report on the Quebec harbour; was his time exclusively given to the work?

Mr. Gobeil is an advocate, practising his profession, and it may be that he did not give his whole time to the work of the department. I do not hold the present minister responsible, because he says his predecessor requested him to employ Mr. Gobeil, but although my hon. friend has tried to cover the matter as cleverly as possible, I believe that Mr. Gobeil, having been the Conservative candidate in Montmorency in 1908, this job was given to him as a reward, and the people of the country have to pay for it.
Has the minister any communication from Mr. Gobeil stating that the work is completed?

Mr. Gobeil has been
sending in reports in connection with the different works at the port of Quebec, such as the special work we are doing in connection with the development of the St. Charles river, which is a very large, a very necessary, and a very important work. These reports will be brought down to the House.

do so.

paid Mr. Ewart, the former chief architect?

raised to $7,000 per annum?
When Mr. Ewart decided he desired to be relieved from the responsible duties of chief architect, *which were growing from year to year, and a new architect had to be secured.
How' long has the new architect been appointed?
About six months.
If we voted only $4,000 for the salary last year, how has he been paid $7,000? Has Mr. Horwood been paid?

Why cannot he be
paid like any otner person who is appointed to office?

Because his name has
to be put in the Estimates.

Why?
' Mr. ROGERS:	Because he has not a
certificate from the Civil Service Commission.
Has the minister asked tne Civil Service Commissioners or either of them to o.k. Mr. Horwood?
Yes.
What did they say?
They refused to do it.
Was there much correspondence about it?
Some.
Was it not on account of that that the minister expressed such virtuous indignation against Mr. Shortt?

I can assure my hon.
friend it was not; I never thought of it.
Will the minister tell me why he was so angry?
I told the House before, while the hon. member was absent.
I read the report in Hansard very carefully, and I could not see any reasonable explanation for such indignation.
The matter was discussed quite shortly.
You are a little short on explanation.	4

There is no doubt that the development of the port of Quebec is important, and that the harbour of Quebec historically is well known in Canada as being one of the most magnificent poTts in this great country of ours. The peculiarity about this report is that to the ordinary man it is a question of engineering, such a report as the minister would get from an engineer. There is some dredging to be done, and it is a question of measurements, of estimating how much earth is to be re- moved and what concrete and supports will be necessary for the piers that are to be constructed at the port. We have a very excellent development of that kind going on in the harbour of Halifax and in the harbour of St. John, but I am not aware that any lawyer has to be engaged to write a history of the harbour of Halifax or of the harbour of St John. I want to bring this matter to the notice of the ministers generally that, while we have very excellent men in the different departments-and I would be sorry to think that we have not good officials capable of discharging the various duties devolving upon them and of furnishing any information that the different departments require-whenever any thing special is to be done under this Administration an outsider must be obtained. In some inquiries that are going on not one thousand miles from this place, it has developed that when anything has to be bought, or anything to be done or any information to be secured, an outsider has always to be secured, and that there is no one in the departments capable of doing the work. That is a sad state of affairs, if it is true.
I do not believe it is true; I believe we have capable officials, and I must bring the blame home to the minister and his brother ministers that this policy is adopted only for the purpose of giving employment to their friends outside. The officials of the different departments are there for the purpose of doing the work pertaining to those departments; but the ministers, in order to widen their sphere of employment, when it is a question of buying binoculars or truck 'wagons, must employ men of large salary and high education, in the legal profession particularly, to do that kind of work. I would be sorry to say a word that would reflect anything but the highest credit upon Mr. Gobeil. I knew him well; he was in the Department of Public Works when I came here first, and a better officer I never came across. He is a good lawyer, and I could understand his being employed by the Minister of Public Works to secure a law library for his department or to write a treatise on titles for land in the province of Quebec-
Or the McGreevy case.

Perhaps it was because he knew too much about the McGreevy case that he was employed; but

to employ a lawyer like himself to make an engineering report is something that I do not quite understand.

Although I think my hon. friend has answered himself, I may say that in so far as Mr. -Gobeil's -standing as a lawyer is concerned, he has never practised his profession at all. He was in the Department of Public Works for over thirty years; he was for ten or twelve years secretary of the department, and he was for seventeen years Deputy Minister of Public Works. Therefore, M-r. Gobeil was the man in Canada who would be most likely to have a proper knowledge where special work was required -and who would be capable of making a report or of giving information -to the department that would be valuable and sound, in view of his long and thorough understanding of the conditions and of the manner in which the department carried on its business. As I understand it, he has made very valuable reports in connection with the different works at Quebec; and, while I have not time to Tead them, I will -see that they are all brought down and laid on the table of the House, so that hon. gentlemen who are interested will have an opportunity of reading them.

Yes.
The minister has not thought it desirable to drop some of the items for the present year so that the amount necessary to be realised may be reduced?

When the Estimates
were prepared this year, we dropped a number of items as they were printed last year. We have included in the Estimates only such items as we are hopeful, if the war should cease and conditions improve, we shall >be able to go on with.

I find in the Auditor
General's Report that a quantity of furni-

ture has been purchased by the Department of Public Works for the different offices in the public buildings. Since the Government came into power, what have they done with the furniture that was there when they -came in? $900 was spent to furnish the office of the Minister of Justice, and about $800 to furnish -the office of the Secretary of State. There must have been some furniture there when the present Government came in.
Goodness knows; perhaps it was -all gone.
What was d-one with it? Was it thrown out or was it given to my hon. friend's friends?
No.
The Department of Public Works bought a rug for the Secretary .of State's office valued at $350.
It must be a mistake.
How bi-g was it?

I do not know. I would like to see that rug. There was purchased from Murray-Kay, Limited, three rugs, one at $385. I said $350; I undervalued it. There is a rug at $85, and another at $49.50. I would like to know the size of that rug valued at $385?
Was it made in Canada?
I do not know whether there is as expensive a rug in Windsor Palace. In the Justice Department there is an item for furniture for the minister's room, $805.
No justice about that.

There is a bookcase, $54; three -chairs, $78.50; clock, $10; davenport, $63; -covering davenport with leather, $35; desk, $135. You can buy a good desk for $50-in fact, for $25. I bought one the other day from the Office Specialty Company, for the office of the school inspector of my county, and I paid only $25.
Was it delivered for that?

The freight from their establishment in Newmarket cost only about a dollar. But this $135 is not all. There is a glass desk-top, $32.85. And the furniture for the minister's room cost $805-two leather chairs, $16.50; three mahogany dinners, $38.85. Does the minister give dinners in his office? For a waste-paper basket we paid $9-you can get one any-

where for half a dollar. When the Liberals were in power we heard about the middleman. But turn to the Auditor General's Report and you will see that under this Government articles to furnish the departments are not bought directly from the manufacturers but from the middlemen. The Government could save 25 per cent or 30 per cent if they dealt with the wholesale men or manufacturers. If it were not that I dislike to take up the time of the committee, I could go through the record of these departments and show that thousands and thousands of dollars have been spent on furniture since this Government come into office. Surely the old furniture was all right. When the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) was Minister of Public Works, if a colleague of his had had come and asked him to pay $385 for a rug, I think he would have thought that colleague was out of his mind. We see now the greatest extravagance that has ever reigned under any Government in this country. Fortunately the Government will have to render an account to the people very soon, and I shall be very much surprised if the voters do not hold them to a very strict account. I can well understand why my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. {Sinclair), when he spoke on the Budget said this Government is spending the money of the people like a lot of drunken sailors. I have been struck with the truth of that expression since I commenced to look into the. Auditor General's Report. On reading these figures I was astounded and disgusted at the extravagance they reveal.

I am sorry that my hon. friend has been so shocked, astounded and pained. I do not know that a fair examination of the accounts will show that the furniture for the Department of Justice or the Department of -the Secretary of State was too expensive. The furniture from those offices, no doubt, was used in otheT offices in the different buildings. That is always the practice; furniture that is old and worn to some extent in the offices of the ministers is removed, and is cleaned up and placed in some other offices with a view to saving as much as we possibly can on this item of furniture.

But I cannot see where they put all the furniture. They have not been opening so many offices as that. Go through the Auditor General's Report for
1914, and you will see the record
9 p.m. of the purchase of many, many articles-desks, chairs, couches; they seem to have a great liking for couches; apparently they have a great disposition to sleep. Even, they have " diners," Do they get their meals brought to their offices? I do not suppose that they are so busy that they could not go to a boarding-house.

What does the term
"dinners" mean?
I could not tell my hon. friend. It must be a clerical error.

Will the minister get
the information?
Yes.
The Minister of Public Works seems more saving for himself than for his colleagues.
Thank you.
He does not sleep.
Perhaps he is not in his office.

The Minister of Marine
and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) has been more saving than the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre), but I find that in his case the Office Specialty Manufacturing Company sold quite -a number of articles for a total of $581.50-mostly office furniture.

I do not find any couches. He does not seem disposed to sleep.
Public Buildings-Ottawa Victoria Memorial Museum, $200,000.
Mr! LEMIEUX: Is that for the tower?

Hon. gentlemen are
familiar with the conditions there: the foundation has been sinking and it is necessary to support it. We have a report from Mr. Monserrat, a copy of which, I believe, has been laid on the table. get along without that. The tower is rather breaking aw-ay from the main building. It is suggested by some that it is dangerous,

It is to be removed.

Only sketch plans.

Not yet.

I think that before we are called upon to pass the preliminary vote we should have some idea of what the Government has in mind. It is hardly right to vote a hundred thousand and not know how many millions we shall have to spend before we stop.
I do not think it will be necessary to go to the millions.
But the principle still holds. Before the Government asks us to launch out on a contract, they ought to give us at least some rough estimate of the expenditure that will be involved.

We are not yet in possession of information that I could give my hon. friend; pending the receipt of reports from the architect and from others in charge of the work, we do not know exactly what the cost will be. We are only going to put up such a building as will meet the requirements of the public interest. I do not think the cost will be more than a million dollars.

I observe that the
Government supply the residences of deputy ministers, secretaries and other officers of the various departments with free telephone service. Is it customary to pay for telephones at the residences of these officials?
It has always been the practice.
On what principle does the Government pay for these telephones?

On the principle that the deputy ministers find it necessary and in the public interest to have telephones at their residences, to be used in connection with their departmental work. It was thought a good many years ago that this would be an advisable extension of the departmental telephone service, and the same practice is carried on to-day.

There might be occasion for a telephone at the residence of a deputy minister, but the other officers of the department are' employed only during the day, and I do not see why their telephones should be paid for.
Harbours and rivers-Esquimau dry dock, $250,000.
What has been done in connection with this work?

We have purchased a site alongside the old dock at Lang's cove. The plans are not yet complete, but when they are ready they will be transmitted to the Admiralty for approval. Only $250,000, therefore, is put in at present for this proposed work.
What is the size of the proposed dry dock?

1,150 feet by 110 feet. The plan of the dock at Quebec is followed as closely as possible.
French river waterway improvements, $500000.
Is it proposed to go ahead with this work during the present year?
This is one of the works that may well, I think, stand for the present year. It is not the intention to press it this year.

I understand that the Minister of Finance looks forward to an expenditure in the neighbourhood of $50,000,000 on capital account for public bn>
Icings and that sort of thing. If I understood the Finance Minister's Budget aright, he expects to raise $30,000,000; about $10,000,000 from the special taxation and about $20,000,000 from the increased duties. If the whole sum of $50,000,000 were expended, the $30,000,000. which I have mentioned would be entirely exhausted, and it would be necessary to borrow besides another $20,000,000. The Minister of Public Works has certain items in the Estimates, the works connected with which he does not intend to proceed with this year. Has

the minister made any estimate as to the amount of these items?

We have not made any such statement as my hon. friend suggests. Our whole estimate of expenditure, including capital account, is only $32,000,000.
Port Arthur and Fort William harbour and river improvements, $1,500,000.
How much has been spent on harbour improvements at Port Arthur and Fort William?
The total expenditure up to March last was $8,500,000.
Is the harbour owned altogether by the Government?

Yes, entirely.
Mr. DEViLIN: With reference to the French river waterway improvements, why is it that the whole of the amount voted last year was not expended?
We were only able to proceed with the dam at Chaudiere last year.

I understood that the
vote was for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.

To some extent that was the purpose of the vote. Practically my hon. friend is right, but all the work we were able to do was the dam.
Public Works-Quebec harbour-dry-dock at Lauzon, $700,000.

When will this dock be
ready?
We did hope that it would be ready this summer. We are now pressing the contractor to get it ready by this fall.
Has the excavation work been started?
It is well under way.
Is the old dry-dock in use at present?
Is that work under way?

Yes. This is to finish it.

What work is going on
under this vote?	*

This is for the wharf that was proposed near Champlain Market. The item was originally in the Railway Estimates as part of the Transcontinental scheme, but it has been transferred to the Public Works Department. The railway part of the scheme has been completed, and we are asking for the money because the wharf is considered necessary.

I do not think we shall

Has any contract been
awarded for this work?

Yes. The contract was
awarded a few years ago by the late Gov-enment.
Has the work been proceeding all this time?

The contract included
the construction of a wharf, and the building of a railway from where the railway crosses the river. Some diversion was made in the contract with the result that the railway end of it was carried out, but not the dock end of it. This item is to enable us to go on with the wharf if necessary.

What is the name of
the contractor?
Davis had the contract.

If I remember rightly
it was intended to erect the terminal of the Transcontinental at the Champlain market, but after a consultation with the engineers we thought that would be a very desirable place for piers for some of the ocean steamers. That is why that amount was provided at that time. I suppose that the changing of the site of the terminal station has modified the views of the Government as to where the improvements should be made?

Yes.
Public Works-Quebec harbour-River St. Charles-improvements to navigation, $500,000.
I would ask the minister to let this item stand until we get the information in regard to Mr. Gobeil's report.

All right.
Item stands.

Public Works-St. John harbour, N.B.-improvements, $1,500,000.

Would die minister
state how the $3,000,000 that was spent last year was divided? What portion was spent on dredging on the west side, how many cubic yards of dredging weTe done, what was the price per cubic yard, what amount of wharf building was done, what was the cost of the temporary warehouses, and how much was spent on the breakwater and on dredging in Courtenay bay?
I have the reports of the officers of the department here, Tout they are" very lengthy. I shall be glad to send them over to my hon. friend.

Perhaps the minister
would hand it to Hansard.
I shall be very glad to do that.

Had Michael Connolly
the contract for any of this work at St. John?
Yes, for the wharves on the west side.
What was the amount of the contract?	.

Something like $1,250,000. The contract was afterwards transferred to the Maritime Dredging Company, who were able to complete the contract in time, and, I think, to the satisfaction of the people of St. John.

What was the reason
for transferring the contract, and how much did Mr. Connolly get for the work he did?

Mr. Connolly received
$605,000 for the portion of the work he did. The department thought he was not likely to complete the contract in time, and so it was handed over to the Maritime Dredging Company, as they were able to carry on the work more speedily.
Does Mr. Connolly claim any extra payment?
No, he was.quite satisfied, I think.

I think that after the
contract was given to the Maritime Dredging Company a change was made in the specifications to permit of substitution of southern timber for Canadian timber, and also change as to the mode in which the crib should be built. I should like to ask whether that is correct, and whether the

new contractors were permitted to substitute a good deal of dredging material in place of rock. I understand that that was permitted.

A change was made in the specifications in regard to timber in order to get the work completed within the time limit. It meant an additional cost of something like $40,000. As to filling, dredged material was used for back filling.
I am told that dredged material was used for filling in the cribs.
No, for back filling only.

What was the cost of
the warehouses?
What is the cost of the temporary warehouse?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The engineer tells me that the whole cost of the warehouse is $27,000.

I would like to ask the
minister if the work performed by Mr. Michael Connolly was accepted by the department as satisfactory? I understand that it was only the question of the delay which caused the transference of the work from Mr. Connolly to the Maritime Dredging Company. I understand that Mr. Connolly is a good contractor.

The principal difficulty was that Mr. Connolly was not proceeding with the work as rapidly as it was thought it should be proceeded with. There was great pressure for the earliest possible completion of this dock in the city of St. John. We were bound to have it completed last fall before the business started and, owing to the reports of the engineers who were sent to examine it, we thought it was going to be impossible, at the rate at which he was carrying on the work, to have it completed in time. That was the reason if was taken from him.

In order to enable the new contractors to hasten the work and finish it in the required time they were allowed, at an extra cost to the department, to substitute southern timber for Canadian timber. Was such a proposal as that ever made to Mr. Connolly to enable him to hurry on the work?
It was impossible to get the local timber in any case, and Mr. Connolly would have had that same right if he had been able to go on and complete the work
Was there any proposal to that effect ever made to Mr. Connolly?
The chief engineer says that before we reached that point it had been taken out of Mr. Connolly's hands because he was not getting on as fast as he should have.

Does not the minister see that Mr. Connolly was treated unjustly, because, according to the minister's own statement, it was impossible to get the matter settled in time to get the timber which was required by the specifications? Without suggesting to Mr. Connolly that he would be allowed to use southern pine, the contract was taken out of his hands because he was not proceeding with sufficient rapidity and it was given to the Maritime Dredging Company and, concurrently with that, the class of timber to be used was changed and they were allowed $40,000 more than Mr. Con. nolly was to get. Does the minister not think that was something of an injustice to Mr. Connolly?

The position was simply this, that we had repeatedly impressed upon Mr. Connolly the necessity of making more rapid progress than he was making with this contract and when the engineers reported that there was no chance of him having it completed in the time prescribed by the contract, an arrangement was made with him by which his work was taken over. He had arranged with others for a local timber but it was discovered that it was utterly impossible to get delivery of the timber and it was absolutely necessary on the part of the new contractor to go on and get the timber in order to have the work completed in time for last year's business. It was a matter that was entirely beyond the control of the department. We could not do anything else to have the work completed and if we had not secured this timber the contract would not have been completed in time.
Was not Mr. Connolly doing the very best possible to get the timber required by the specifications when the contract was taken out of his hands?
I do not know; he may have been doing that, but he was not getting on with the work as fast as the department thought he should.

What happened? It was taken out of his hands, given to new contractors, and they were at once told that
they need not carry out the specifications, that they could get timber different from that which Mr. Connolly was obliged to get. When they got the timber that they could get more easily than the timber required by the specifications, the department allowed the new contractors an extra sum of $40,000. They allowed him to get timber which it was easier to get, and they paid him $40,000 more.

That was not exactly the case. The representations which prompted the department to make the change in the timber came from the city of St. John itself. The city of St. John pressed this upon the Government. Understanding the local conditions, they brought to the attention of the department the fact that the only hope of having the contract completed was by getting the class of timber that we did get in order to carry on the work.
Mr, PUGSLEY: I have understood that Mr. Connolly's complaint-and he makes a very strong complaint-is that he was not given the same chance as the new contractors were given. If he had been allowed to substitute southern timber he could have got along just as rapidly as the new contractors did. However, I suppose the minister has said all he can upon it. I would like to ask as to the depth of the dredging which has been done upon the west side.
Thirty-two feet.
And for the crib site?
Thirty-five feet.
Has there been no dredging done outside of the crib site to thirty-five feet?
The engineer says that he has no knowledge of such.

I would like to mention this fact for the minister's information: Other gentlemen were formerly interested in the Maritime Dredging Company who were the previous contractors. They conferred with me about going to a depth of thirty-five feet. I thought that, not only for the crib site but for the basin, it was desirable to dredge to a depth of thirty-five feet, and I so authorized the engineer, Mr. Scammell. I expected to have an Order in Council passed giving authority for this work. I understand that the dredging to a depth of thirty-five feet was done, but it has not been paid for by reason of it being alleged that the company went below depth.

My own view. is that as there is considerable silting in the harbour it would be desirable to go to a sufficient depth to avoid the necessity of dredging again in the near, future. Has the minister's attention been called to that claim?

I have no recollection of ever having had my attention called to that particular matter. I quite appreciate what my hon. friend says in regard to the matter of silting in the harbour of St. John, and in my judgment care should be taken to see that the depth should be great enough. At all events, I shall be very glad to look into the matter that the hon. gentleman refers to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Has any claim been put in?
There has been a claim put in. Mr. James A. Bulyea was in Ottawa and saw me in reference to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He did not see me. I have never heard anything albout any claim being made.
He was here for some days and endeavoured to get the matter settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I never saw him.
Mr. PUGSLEY': I thought he would have seen the minister.
I shall be very glad to look into it.

I am pleased to hear the minister say that. I feel a certain amount of responsibility in connection with it, for the reason that perhaps I ought to have expedited it before the late Government went out of office and had the Order m Council passed. Mr. Scammell held the opinion that it was very desirable to dredge to that depth in the basin. Has it been arranged that the drydock should be of the same dimensions as those which will be built at Quebec and Esquimalt?

My hon. friend is familiar with the original conditions under which a dry dock of 900 feet was proposed, but the department suggested a dry dock of 1,150 feet similar to those at Halifax and Quebec. This has been brought to ihe attention of the Norton Griffiths Company, the contractors, but they have not yet signified their willingness to carry it out. The matter is now under consideration, and I believe will be adjusted. I am free to ac-

knowledge that undoubtedly the port of St. John ought to have and must have a dry dock of similar size to those at Halifax and Quebec.

I am very glad indeed to hear the statement of the minister, because I think it would be desirable to build a dry dock of 1,150 feet at St. John, not merely that it may be as larve as those at Quebec and Esquimalt and Halifax, but because of the convenience of dividing it into sections so that vessels of different sizes can be taken care of to advantage. A great deal of shipping comes to the port of St. John, and the business is increasing every year. I think the minister will make no mistake if he arranges for a dry dock of a larger size.

My idea was that I did not regard it as fair that the port of St. John should have a smaller dry dock than that in Quebec or in Halifax, because I felt that ships which require the largest possible 'dry dock should have the same opportunity of coming to St. John as they would have to Halifax and Quebec. I thought, therefore, in fairness to the port of St. John, that it should have a dry dock of the same size.

When the late Government laid down the policy of assisting in the construction of dry docks by giving an annual subsidy for a period of years, the different (ports were placed in the same position and it was anticipated that dry docks should be built by companies. With this understanding, the different ports had the same opportunity, through private enterprise, of securing the construction of dry docks, but now that the Government is determined to build dry docks as Government works at Quebec and Halifax, which are, of course, competing ports with St, John, the minister can easily see that a difficulty would be thrown in the way of a dry dock being constructed at St. John by private enterprise. Of course, Government dty docks have the advantages of cheap rates which the Government necessarily feels called upon to give to those using the docks, and a dock owned by a private company is not nearly so likely to be a successful enterprise, as it would if it were in competition only with eompany-owned docks. I would like the minister to consider that circumstance, and perhaps he may decide that it would be desirable to construct the dry dock at St. John as a Government work,

as the dry docks at Halifax, Quebec and Esquimalt are being constructed.

There is a good deal of force in the suggestion of my hon. friend, but at the same time I find myself in the position of having a contract with a reputable company for the carrying out of the construction of this particular dry dock at St. John, and I do not know that it would he possible to make any change. However, the matter will be fully considered.
Toronto harbour improvements, $1,000,000.
I understood they were to dredge in the bay there, and deposit the material taken out on the shore.
That is quite right.
Have they done much of that work?

They are building their dredges, and will get started very shortly.
Vancouver harbour improvements, $1,000,000.
What is this vote for?
It is for a very important public wharf between Salisbury and Commercial streets.
We voted $1,000,000 last year, and there is this year $1,000,000, which seems a great deal of money for a wharf whei e there is no dredging to be done. What is the length of the wharf?
800 feet long and 300 feet wide.
800 feet oat in the water?
Yes, and the vote includes dredging at False creek as well.
Is it a concrete wharf?
Yes.
Any British Columbia pine in it?

Yes, there is some in the foundations.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Has the Halifax dry-dock been taken over by the Government?

The proposed new dry dock has nothing to do with the old dry dock.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Is it near where the old dry dock was?

It is across the Hver on the Dartmouth side, which was selected by the engineers as the most suitable.
Public buildings-Nova Scotia, $365,000.
These are just the same Estimates as were passed last year; there is nothing new in them.
I wish to ask a question about the Amherst post office. What was the cost of the site?
What is the size of the lot?

It is only fair to say to the minister that my information is that that land was purchased by some parties not very long ago, before it was acquired by the Government, for $15,000, and the Government decided to take the property and. build a new post office. Expropriation proceedings were commenced; but when the case was about to come to trial, the Crown settled with the owners at $30,000, the price which the minister named. That was double what the property cost the purchasers a comparatively short time before and after there was an agitation for the erection of a new post office. $30,000 seems a very high price for the property.

Inasmuch as the matter
refers to my constituency and has been brought up by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) perhaps I may be permitted to say a word or two. There is nothing in the record of the department to show the price paid for the land by the vendor to the Government. As a matter of fact, there is no secret about it. I think the price is somewhat in the neighbourhood of $$16,000 to $17,000. That is what it represented to the vendor in his outlay plus interest.

The party purchased for $16,000 or $17,000 the property for which the Crown paid $30,000. That would represent a profit to the vendor of some $13,000. What is the name of the gentleman who made the profit of $13,000?

Mr. H. G. Hagen. This information is, I believe, accurate. The whole point is whether or not the Government paid a fair price for the land, and speaking for myself, I have absolutely no doubt that the Government got the land at a fair and reasonable price. The site is in the heart of the town of Amherst, which has a population of about 11,000, and which, if it continues to grow at the rate at which it was growing two years ago, will in 1920 have

a population of about 20,000. The price paid for the land represents $325 per front foot, with a depth of 93 feet. There is also in the rear a right of way 12 feet wide, which practically means that the lot is 105 feet in depth for the purpose of the post office. Land immediately in front of this site has been purchased by people for their own use as a business site. In one instance a lot 75 feet in depth was purchased a year before by a merchant who paid $525 per front foot. In another case, within nine months of the purchase of this piece of land by the Government, a lot 50 feet in depth, without any right of way at the rear opposite this lot and not more than 75 feet down the street, was bought by a merchant for $450 per front foot for his own private use. Perhaps land upon the side of the street on which this lot is situated is not quite as valuable as it is on the other side; but for the purpose of a post office site to the Government, it is quite as valuable and possibly more so, inasmuch at it is hoped to use the old post office building for a customs house and the new post office is to be used for the post office, and both being upon the same side of the street, it will enable a more advantageous exchange of parcels between the post office and the customs house and vice versa. With respect to the question whether a post office ought to be built or not, I think that matter was gone into last year. The Post Office Department itself felt, even before the parcel post system was installed, which called for additional room, that the business of the town was growing so rapidly that the post office was crowded, and it asked the Public Works Department for an increase in facilities. An engineer was sent down, through no effort of my own, but as a matter of departmental routine, and he prepared a plan which, according to his own estimate, called for the expenditure of $40,000, although it meant simply an addition to the existing building and only a makeshift which would provide for the needs of the town for only a short time and which would not be sufficient for the accommodation which the growth would call for in a few years. Therefore, it was felt that, instead of spending $40,000 and having post office accommodation which would last only a few years, and inferior accommodation for the customs house, it would be better to spend a few more thousand dollars and have first-class accommodation for both the pest office and the customs. Therefore it 
is in the public interest that the department has decided upon the erection of a new post office.

How long before the
Government expropriated this property was it that Mr. Hazen bought the site for $16,000?
Mr. RHODES; Perhaps six or nine months. I am speaking from memory, and I have had no occasion to refresh my memory.

Some six or nine months before the Government expropriated the property, it had been bought by this gentleman for an amount which my hon. friend says with interest would reach $16,000 or $17,000, and the Government paid this gentleman something over $30,000 for it. Before I left office, there was an order, which I feel sure is on record in the department, that all examiners must state any recent transfers of property which had been purchased.
That was carried out.
[DOT] My hon. friend said there was no record in the department of the cost. Therefore it could not have been carried out.
I had not that in mind at the time I was speaking, but I am inclined to think it will be found that the report of the inspector will disclose the cost.

I gave a general order
to the inspector that all examiners must state any recent transfers of property which had been purchased. Will the minister be good enough to produce the report of the examiner at a convenient time before these Estimates finally pass?

We shall be glad to produce any reports we have, but an error appears to have crept in here. This particular property was expropriated by the department. The matter was referred to the Exchequer Court, and the price of $385 per foot was fixed by the judge of the Exchequer Court, not by the department.
My information is that the price was settled by agreement.
My information is that it was fixed by the Exchequer Court.
The order was passed by consent. I remember seeing it at the time the court was sitting in Halifax.
That is a pretty big profit.
When the department referred the matter to the Exchequer Court and the order came back placing a value of $30,000 on the property we had not any more to say.
Surely the counsel for the Crown would not consent to have a valuation without consulting the minister.

When this property was valued by the officers of the Public Works Department, they set a value of $325 a foot. It was referred to the Exchequer Court, and after the judge had given, it consideration, he came to the conclusion that the price suggested by the officer of $325 a foot was fair and reasonable, and that was his finding.
I think the minister is misinformed. My information is that the judge passed no judgment, but the counsel for the Crown accepted this price:

I know something of the circumstances of this case. As a matter of fact, the Government inspectors and valuators were convinced that the price was fair and reasonable, as I was and am. But I found out, when the purchase was proposed to be made, that the price which had been paid by the vendor was a good deal different from the price which he was about to receive from the Government, and I suggested that the matter be sent to the Exchequer Court. *My letter will probably be found on the files. I said, that while I had no doubt as to the value of the land, yet, in order to avoid all suspicion, I should like to see the question go to the Exchequer Court. At the sittings of the court held in Halifax last autumn, the case was called and a number of witnesses were there ready to proceed. Judge Cassels was presiding. He asked what was the point in the case; and the counsel for the Government-who was not the man it had been proposed should represent the Government, but, I believe, had been called in a very short time before the case was heard-said that the Government had offered $325 a front foot, but the vendor was asking something like $400 a foot. The judge said: " I think that $325 a foot is a reasonable price," or something of that kind, and suggested that the vendor should accept it. There was a conference, and the vendor agreed to accept the price, and judgment went on that ground.
Without evidence?

One witness was called as a matter of fact. So far as I am concerned,
I welcome any inquiry with regard to this land; there is no mystery about
10 p.m. it. I have no hesitation in going on record as saying that I believe the Government got good value for its money.
What is the population?
Eleven thousand, and growing rapidly.

No, for the same reason that other towns are not growing-for the same reason that the city of Montreal is not growing. And I want to say, what hon. members know full well, that many towns in other parts of Canada, especially towns in the West, having only half the population .of Amherst, would think that land was going ridiculously cheap if as good sites as this were bought within their borders for $325 a foot.
It is an unfortunate thing, when hon: gentlemen wanted to go to the Exchequer Court to allay suspicion, that they did not allow evidence in the matter.

That was for the judge to
say.

The counsel for the
Crown consented to pay $325 a food. Will the minister please bring down the information that has been asked for?

That armoury cost about $2,000, and there ought to be a better building there. The drill hall is in use to-day.
That is what I want to know.

It has been used for weeks past as an instructional school for officers for overseas contingents. Every day it is being used in connection with the mobilization of troops. We have the honour to have in the town of Amherst at the present

time the 22nd French Canadian regiment, and perhaps I may be permitted to say, for the benefit of our friends from the province of Quebec, that the people of Amherst are delighted with the physique and the appearance of the men of this regiment. Every letter I receive is loud in its praises of the men, not only as soldiers, but as men; their conduct has been exemplary in every respect.

I thank the hon. member for his kind comment. It is natural that the men from the province of Quebec-I except, of course, present company-should be men of fine physique. We are glad to know that the French Canadians have visited the town of Amherst. Can the hon. gentleman tell me how many officers use that drill hall?

There are probably 150 officers in the town at the present time. The 22nd French Canadian regiment, which is composed almost entirely of Roman Catholics, has not had a building sufficiently large for the purposes of worship, and they have been using the building on Sundays for church purposes. It has been used also for quartermaster's stores; I believe, that every inch of space in the building has been used for weeks past in connection with the presence in the town of the 22nd French Canadian regiment.	.
The Minister of Militia informed the House that a portion of the factory buildings had .been rented by the Government for the purposes of the troops.

The minister did not inform the House any such thing. No rent is being paid; no one has been asked for the payment of rent, and no one is expected to pay it. There will be, I presume, small payments for such damage as has been done to the building and any expense to which the company has been put by reason of the occupation, but this compensation will be small.

That is a matter which comes under the control of the Militia Department.

The minister will remember that a rather interesting story was told, I think by the hon. member for Richmond, in regard to this matter last session. He pointed out that Sir Frederick Borden had offered a free site which, if I remember the story correctly, was in a suitable place in the town of Canning. This site was approved at a public meeting held in the town; Sir Frederick Borden was thanked for his generous, offer and a description of the site was sent to the minister, who acknowledged receipt of the offer. It appears, however, that certain political friends of one Mr. Eaton were anxious that a site should be purchased from him, and I understand that the department was pressed to conclude a bargain with Mr. Eaton for the purchase from him of a piece of land which many of the inhabitants 125J
thought was entirely unsuitable for the purpose. Mr. Eaton was to receive $2,000 for this site. The department offered Sir Frederick Borden $1,100 for the strip of land which was to be added to Mr. Eaton's land, but Sir , Frederick said that $1,100 was altogether too much. He refused the offer, and I understand that a suit as to the value of the land was brought by the department and defended by Sir Frederick Borden.
. Evidently the reason why the department was pushing the $1,100 on Sir Frederick was, as they said in the correspondence, to take the curse off the Eaton lot.
As they had estimated the lot adjoining Sir Frederick's at $2,000, they thought Sir Frederick should be paid proportionally $1,100 for his strip. I understand Sir Frederick resisted the offer and went to law about it with the department. It would be interesting to know the result of that trial. Has it been settled yet?
It has not been settled, at all. I am not acquainted with the details, but I know that no suit has been brought in the Exchequer Court.

I should like to know what the policy of the department is in regard to post office buildings. I understand that Canning is a village of only 500 or 600 people, yet here is an appropriation for a public building there costing $15,000. Prior to 1911 a site was purchased by the late Government for a post office in the town of Camrose in my own constituency. It is a very thriving little place with a population of 2,000, and with all the modern facilities that are to be found in our western towns. I have repeatedly asked the Minister of Public Works for a building suitable to the requirements of the town, but I can get no satisfaction whatever. Camrose has seven railways radiating from it, and yet the post office is located in a rented building, although the Government has had a site purchased ever since 1910. It looks to me as if the erection of public buildings was merely a political move, and this is rather a glaring case. Without any reason or justification whatever, the demands of the progressive people of a flourishing little town like Camrose are ignored and places with one-tenth the

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Electric lighting.
I understand that tenders were recently called for electric lighting?
Yes.

I understand that the lowest tenderer has been urging that changes ought to be made which would make his work less expensive, and I am sure the minister will agree with me that it would not be fair to make any changes without calling for new tenders. I think the contractor ought to be compelled to adhere to the original specifications on which he tendered, and if changes are to be made thep, tenders should be called for again. I

mention this especially to the minister so that his attention may be called to it.

Tenders were called for and the contract has been let to the lowest tenderer and a certain amount of work has been done by the contractor. He now represents that the specifications wer-e not what they should be and he came to Ottawa and I looked into the matter myself with the result that I have sent the chief electrician to St. John to make a report on the conditions, so that we can decide what is best to be done in the public interest.

I am sure the minister will agree with me that if a contractor cannot perform his contract the work should be taken from him and new tenders called. There should be no encouragement given to men to tender below what they think the work is worth, in the hope that they may be able to induce the department to make it easier for them later. That apparently is what the contractor is seeking in this case. The others tendered on the understanding that they would be compelled to carry out the specifications to the letter. When I was minister the rule I adopted was that if any changes were to be made the contract should be cancelled and the work let out again to tender, and given to the lowest.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: My information is that there would be a very marked difference in the cost of doing the work if these changes are made which are asked for by the gentleman who was the lowest tenderer. I am also informed that other tenderers inquired of the chief architect as to whether any changes would be allowed, and pointing out the changes which they thought desirable to make, i*nd which could be made without disadvantage, and the chief architect informed one or more of them by wire that no changes would be permitted, and that the work must be done strictly in accordance with the specifications. These gentlemen tendered accordingly. The Minister of Marine must see how unfair it would be_to the others who tendered if these changes were allowed to be made to the advantage of the lowest tenderer. If any changes are to be made the work should again be put up to competition.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am simply telling my hon. friend the statements which have been made to me in regard to the matter. The price of the lowest tenderer was just about one-half of that of most of the other tenderers. There was another company which tendered from the city of Ottawa, which was just a few hundred dollars higher than the lowest tenderer which was selected. The gentleman who was awarded the contract states that he is perfectly prepared to carry on the work according to the specifications and that he has no desire to toe relieved of the contract, because he will make a fair margin of profit on it. But, he thinks in view of the strong representations made to him toy the officials in St. John, he ought to report the matter to the Department of Public Works before proceeding.
If the minister decides to make these changes, in all fairness the work should be put up to tender again and the present contractor paid for what work lie has done.
My hon. friend will admit that I have taken the proper course by sending the chief electrician to St. John, and when I get his report I will give it my best consideration.

That is all I ask of the minister.

As I do not wish to take up the time of the committee unnecessarily, I shall not insist further. I stand by my protest and am thankful to the minister for the hope he holds out for the future.
